**Fireside Address from the Oval Office, Delivered January 21, 2025**  
My fellow Americans,  
I’m speaking to you tonight from behind the Resolute Desk, where a log crackles in the fireplace, the coffee’s gone lukewarm in my favorite chipped mug, and I’ve got a scuffed 1986 dime sitting between my thumb and forefinger. I fished it out of the lining of my winter coat this morning—must’ve been tucked there since I knocked on doors in Des Moines back in 2020, covered in snow, shaking hands with a grandma who pressed a handful of change into my palm for a cup of hot cocoa. If you’ve got a dime in your pocket right now, or tucked in a couch cushion, or rolling around the bottom of your purse, you might be wondering: what good is 10 lousy cents these days? Can’t buy a soda, can’t buy a stamp, can barely buy a gumball at the corner mall. Let me tell you: that dime is one of the most powerful things you own. And I’ve got some advice for what to do with it.

First, let’s remember who’s on that dime. Franklin Delano Roosevelt, the man who led us through the Great Depression and a world war, who contracted polio at 39 and spent most of his adult life walking with steel braces, hidden from the public so no one would mistake vulnerability for weakness. In 1938, with polio ravaging American kids, filling hospital wards with iron lungs and leaving thousands of children paralyzed every year, FDR launched the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis. He didn’t beg billionaires for seven-figure checks. He asked every single American to send one dime to the White House. In the first week alone, 2.8 million dimes flooded the mailroom—stuffed in crumpled envelopes, taped to postcards, sent by kids who’d shined shoes after school, by secretaries who’d dug change out of their purses on their lunch break, by farmers who’d traded a dozen eggs for pocket change to send. That flood of dimes funded the research that created the Salk vaccine, eradicated polio in the United States by 1979, and saved millions of lives. That dime you’re holding? It’s not just copper and nickel. It’s a monument to what ordinary people can do when they show up with what little they have.

First piece of advice: Give it away. Not to a big national charity (though that’s fine too), but to the first person you see who’s just a little short. Tomorrow, when you’re at the grocery store, or the coffee shop, or the bus stop, watch for the kid digging through his backpack for change to buy a $1.10 lemonade who only has a crumpled dollar. Watch for the veteran fumbling through his wallet for that last 10 cents for a bottle of water after a long day at the VA. Watch for the single mom counting change at the checkout line, holding a toddler who’s begging for a 10-cent sticker by the register. Hand them that dime, smile, and say “No need to pay me back.” That dime doesn’t just cover 10 cents. It tells that person they’re seen. That they’re not alone. Abraham Lincoln talked about the “better angels of our nature” — that dime is your way of calling on those angels, of tying your story to a stranger’s in a small, quiet, perfect act of grace. That’s the social contract, folks: not just laws written in Congress, but millions of small, uncelebrated choices to look out for each other.

Second: Invest it in someone you’ll never meet. Open a custodial savings account for the kid down the street, for your niece, for a foster kid in your community, and drop that dime in it. Let’s do the math: a single dime, compounded at 7% annual return (the historical average for the stock market, adjusted for inflation), will be worth nearly $87 in 100 years. If you add a dime every month for the next 18 years, that kid will have almost $500 when they go to college — enough for textbooks, a bus pass, groceries their first semester away from home. John F. Kennedy said we chose to go to the moon not because it was easy, but because it was hard, because it would measure the best of our energies. That dime is your own small moonshot. We built the interstate highway system, the public schools, the land-grant colleges for people we’d never meet. This is your chance to do the same, one 10-cent piece at a time.

Third: If you want to keep it, keep it as a reminder. So many of us walk around thinking we don’t have enough to give, enough to make a difference. We think change only comes from presidents, from billionaires, from celebrities. That dime is proof that’s a lie. The Montgomery Bus Boycott was funded by dimes and quarters pooled by maids and teachers who walked 5 miles to work every day rather than ride a segregated bus. The suffragettes sold 10-cent “Votes for Women” pins to fund their marches for the ballot. Every big, world-changing movement in this country started with ordinary people giving what little they had, one dime at a time. Keep that dime on your desk, in your wallet, on your nightstand. When you’re feeling small, when you’re feeling like your voice doesn’t matter, hold it in your hand and remember: 10 cents from 28 million people cured polio. What could you do, with whatever you have, no matter how small?

And fourth? If you want to spend it on something silly, something just for you? Do it. No guilt. This country wasn’t built so we could all be miserable martyrs. It was built so we could pursue happiness, remember? If you’ve worked a 12-hour shift, if you’ve been caring for a sick kid, if you’ve just had a terrible day, take that dime, go to the corner store, buy a gumball, and savor every bite. That small joy is not a waste. It’s fuel. You can’t pour from an empty cup, and a nation of people who never let themselves have a small, silly joy can’t do the hard work of building a better country. When I was a kid, my dad gave me a dime every time I helped a neighbor carry groceries, every time I did a chore without being asked. I saved up 10 dimes and bought my little sister a lollipop and a drawing pad for her 5th birthday. That was the first time I realized that small things add up to something that matters.

That dime you’re holding? It’s a choice. A choice to care, to invest, to remember, to celebrate. That’s what this country is, after all: not a collection of monuments or famous names, but millions of small choices, every day, by ordinary people, doing what they can with what they have. So whatever you do with your dime, do it with purpose, do it with pride, and remember: you don’t need to be a president, a millionaire, or a hero to change the world. You just need a dime, and a heart willing to use it.

God bless you, and God bless the United States of America.

# How a Clear, Flexible Schedule Makes Your Parenting Plan Actually Work

You may have to meet with a helper to work out a parenting plan. The first step would be to estimate how much time you have every day for parenting, and is that enough to cover the hands-on support, active engagement, and logistical coordination your children need to thrive? For many caregivers—whether separated co-parents navigating shared custody, two-career households balancing demanding workloads, or extended families splitting care duties—bringing in a neutral, trained helper (often a certified parenting coordinator or family support specialist) takes the friction out of negotiating expectations, ensuring no one person bears an unfair share of the work.

Once you’ve completed your initial time audit, accounting for both structured responsibilities like homework help and unstructured connection time, the next and most critical phase of building your plan is drafting a schedule. A thoughtfully crafted schedule eliminates the last-minute texts, tense negotiations, and unspoken resentment that so often arise when care responsibilities are left unwritten. A good schedule doesn’t just assign logistical tasks like school drop-offs, extracurricular pickups, or tutoring coordination to specific caregivers; it also carves out intentional, unstructured time for connection, whether that’s a weekly hike on local trails, a board game night, or a low-pressure check-in to talk through social stressors at school.

Your helper will first walk you through mapping every non-negotiable commitment each caregiver has—from recurring work meetings to longstanding personal obligations—before slotting parenting duties into the schedule. This ensures the schedule is rooted in reality, not idealized expectations of what you think you should be able to handle. For example, if one caregiver has a mandatory team meeting every Wednesday afternoon that runs right through school dismissal, that time can be assigned to the other caregiver or a trusted backup, so no one is forced to choose between their career and their care responsibilities.

One common pitfall many caregivers fall into is building a schedule that is too rigid, with no room for life’s unexpected shifts: a child’s last-minute invitation to a classmate’s celebration, a sudden work project that requires extra hours, or a last-minute school field trip that needs a chaperone. Your helper will encourage you to build small buffer windows into the schedule, and to outline clear, low-stakes processes for swapping shifts or adjusting responsibilities when needed, so no one feels penalized when routine is disrupted. They will also likely recommend hosting the schedule on a shared digital platform, where every caregiver can access real-time updates, note upcoming events like science fairs or sports playoffs, and request swaps without needing to have a tense one-on-one conversation.

Many caregivers push back at first, arguing that a schedule strips the joy and spontaneity out of parenting. But the opposite is true: when everyone knows exactly what they are responsible for, and no one is carrying the mental load of tracking every unassigned task, there is far more room for spontaneous fun. A caregiver who doesn’t have to wonder if they need to rearrange their workday to cover an unplanned commitment can easily agree to a last-minute trip to the local arcade after homework, because they know their other responsibilities are already accounted for in the shared plan.

Your helper will also walk you through setting a regular cadence to revisit and revise the schedule as your family’s needs change. A schedule that works perfectly for an 8-year-old in elementary school will not work for a 15-year-old with after-school club commitments, a part-time job, and late study sessions for upcoming exams. Quarterly check-ins, guided by your helper, give everyone a chance to voice concerns, adjust for new obligations, and make sure the schedule still feels equitable for every caregiver and meets the needs of every child.

At the end of the process, your parenting plan will be far more than a list of rules: it will be a living document centered on a schedule that prioritizes both your children’s sense of security and your well-being as a caregiver. The helper’s role is not to dictate terms, but to facilitate conversations that center everyone’s needs, so your schedule works for your unique family, not a one-size-fits-all idea of what parenting should look like.

Proposal for Research into Language Evolution Dynamics in Geographically Separated Speech Groups

This project addresses a key gap in current understandings of how language evolves over multiple generations. Most existing work on language evolution draws from printed texts or short term speech samples that fail to track subtle gradual shifts that unfold across decades. Many studies also focus on widely spoken languages with large speaker bases that have regular exposure to mass media and cross group interaction. Those conditions mask the core internal drivers of evolution that operate when speech groups are shielded from external influence. No prior work has isolated those drivers by comparing highly similar groups that differ only in their level of interaction with outside populations.

This project will fill that gap by tracking language evolution across three generations in two nearly identical speech groups that live on separate small islands in the North Atlantic. Both groups share the same ancestral language root and have nearly equal population size and proximity to equivalent material resources. The only key difference between the two groups is that one has had no regular interaction with mainland populations for 80 years while the other established regular monthly ferry links to the mainland 40 years prior to the start of the study.

Over the course of five years the research team will collect 120 hours of recorded informal speech from 60 participants total split evenly across the two groups and across three age bands of 18 to 30 31 to 50 and 51 plus. The team will partner with local island leadership to secure participant agreement and ongoing community support for all data gathering activities. Each participant will complete a series of structured speaking tasks that prompt use of descriptive terms narrative structure and response to hypothetical scenarios. The team will also collect observation notes from group public events such as town meetings and seasonal festivals to document speech used in natural unprompted settings. All recorded speech will be transcribed and tagged for shifts in lexical selection syntactic structure pronunciation of vowel and speech sound patterns and use of novel phrases that emerge during the study window. The team will compare shift rates and shift types between the two groups and across generations to identify which shifts stem from external interaction and which arise from internal group dynamics independent of outside influence.

This project will produce new insight into the mechanisms that drive language evolution over relatively short time frames. It will also generate a large open shared dataset of natural speech that future researchers can use to explore additional questions related to language variation and evolution. Findings from the study will inform work in fields ranging from linguistic anthropology to speech pathology to educational design for multilingual learner groups. The study will also set a framework for longer term monitoring of the two groups to track evolution across additional future generations.

First, the easy answer: Avocado is not a fish. Salmon is a widely consumed oily cold-water fish, while avocados are creamy, single-seeded berries native to Mesoamerica. What makes this pair so fascinating is that despite being completely unrelated in biology, they are one of the most beloved culinary matches of the modern era.

To start with salmon: These MIGRATORY creatures have one of the most dramatic life cycles on Earth. Born in tiny, ice-cold freshwater streams, they travel thousands of miles out to the open ocean to mature for 2 to 7 years, feeding on krill and small fish that give their flesh its signature deep orange hue. When they reach reproductive age, they navigate back to the exact stream they hatched in to spawn, often climbing 100+ foot waterfalls and evading bears and eagles along the way. Long a staple for Indigenous communities across the Northern Hemisphere, salmon is prized nutritionally for its high-quality protein and OMEGA-3 fatty acids, which support long-term heart and brain health. Today, roughly 70% of salmon sold globally is farmed, raised in either ocean net pens or closed land-based systems to reduce pressure on vulnerable wild populations.

Avocados, by contrast, grow on broad-leafed evergreen trees in subtropical and tropical climates. Cultivated by Indigenous communities in Mexico and Guatemala for more than 7,000 years, the global avocado market is now dominated by the HASS variety, first patented by a California postal worker in 1935. Hass avocados’ thick, bumpy skin that turns deep purple when ripe made them far easier to ship and ripen at home than smoother, lighter-skinned heirloom varieties, launching them to global stardom by the 1990s. Unlike most fruits, avocados are high in heart-healthy monounsaturated fat rather than sugar, giving them their rich, buttery texture that makes them a versatile ingredient in everything from dips to smoothies.

The magic of the salmon and avocado pairing lies in their perfect balance of texture and flavor. Salmon’s flaky, briny, savory flesh packed with UMAMI cuts right through avocado’s mild, creamy, subtly sweet richness, creating a bite that feels indulgent but light at the same time. The combination first blew up in the 1960s, when California sushi chefs invented the California roll as an accessible, Western-friendly take on traditional sushi. They used avocado as a creamy stand-in for hard-to-source fatty toro (tuna belly), and before long, chefs began adding salmon to the roll to amp up the savory depth. Today, the pair appears on menus worldwide: in poke bowls stacked with marinated salmon and cubed avocado, on crispy toast topped with seared salmon and sliced avocado, even in bright, fresh salsas served alongside grilled salmon filets.

Both salmon and avocados are NUTRIENT-DENSE staples, but both face pressing sustainability challenges. Wild salmon populations have declined by more than 50% in some regions due to dam construction that blocks spawning paths, habitat degradation, and overfishing. Avocado farming is extremely water-intensive: it takes roughly 2,000 liters of water to grow 1 kilogram of avocados, putting massive strain on drought-prone growing regions like central Mexico and southern California. That’s why choosing SUSTAINABLE sourced versions of both foods is a small, impactful choice for shoppers: for salmon, look for third-party certifications from groups like the Marine Stewardship Council, and for avocados, seek out brands that use rainwater harvesting and regenerative farming practices to reduce water use.

In the end, it’s a delightful quirk of global food culture that two organisms with such wildly different lives—one that swims across entire oceans, one that grows on sun-warmed trees—have come together to be one of the most universally loved food pairings on the planet.

<<Kotlin vs Java: Key Pros and Cons for Software Development>>
Both are statically typed, JVM-first programming languages, with Java (launched 1995 by Sun Microsystems) serving as the foundation for enterprise, Android, and backend development for decades, and Kotlin (launched 2011 by JetBrains) designed as a Java-compatible modern alternative that Google named the preferred language for Android development in 2019. Below is a structured comparison of their relative pros and cons:
### Pros of Kotlin (vs Java)
1. **Built-in null safety**: Kotlin distinguishes between nullable and non-nullable types at compile time, eliminating ~90% of NullPointerException (NPE) errors—the most common runtime bug in Java. Java’s Optional class is a clunky, optional workaround that does not enforce null safety at the language level.
2. **Dramatically reduced boilerplate**: Features like data classes (auto-generate `equals()`, `hashCode()`, `toString()`, and accessors for POJOs), default/named parameters, and type inference cut lines of code for equivalent functionality by 40–60% compared to Java, reducing maintenance overhead and human error. No third-party tools like Lombok are required to cut redundant code.
3. **Mature coroutines for async work**: Kotlin’s lightweight, structured concurrency model simplifies asynchronous and concurrent code, and is far more flexible and less resource-heavy than Java’s traditional threads or even Java 21’s newer virtual threads. Coroutines integrate seamlessly with Android, backend frameworks, and cross-platform tools.
4. **Modern quality-of-life features**: Extension functions let developers add new functionality to existing classes (e.g. `String`, `List`) without modifying source code or using clunky utility classes, a feature Java entirely lacks. Smart casts automatically narrow types after type checks, eliminating the explicit casting required for Java’s `instanceof` checks.
5. **Interoperability and multiplatform support**: Kotlin is 100% compatible with existing Java code, libraries, and frameworks, allowing teams to migrate incrementally without rewriting entire codebases. Additionally, Kotlin Multiplatform enables cross-platform development for JVM, iOS, Android, web, and native desktop, a use case Java cannot support natively.
6. **Enforced immutability controls**: Built-in `val` (immutable reference) and `var` (mutable reference) keywords enforce immutability by default more consistently than Java’s `final` keyword, which is often underused or inconsistently applied.
### Cons of Kotlin (vs Java)
1. **Slower clean compilation**: While incremental builds are roughly on par with Java, full clean builds of large Kotlin codebases are 10–30% slower than equivalent Java codebases, increasing latency for CI/CD pipelines and large enterprise deployments.
2. **Steeper learning curve**: Kotlin’s blend of object-oriented and functional programming features, null safety rules, coroutines, and extension functions create a steeper learning curve for developers only familiar with Java’s procedural, verbose syntax. Pitfalls like platform types (nullable/non-nullable ambiguity when calling Java code) can lead to unexpected bugs for new Kotlin developers.
3. **Smaller talent pool and ecosystem**: Java’s 28-year head start means it has a far larger global developer community, more extensive documentation, more battle-tested third-party library support, and a deeper pool of senior talent for hire. Many niche enterprise libraries are only tested or officially supported for Java.
4. **Single-vendor governance risk**: Kotlin is primarily developed and supported by JetBrains, a single commercial company, whereas Java has multiple independent long-term support (LTS) providers (Oracle, OpenJDK, Amazon Corretto, Azul) offering 8+ years of support per version. This creates higher vendor lock-in risk for enterprise teams relying on long-term system stability.
5. **Occasional performance overhead**: Implicit boxing of primitive types (Kotlin treats all values as objects by default) and extra bytecode generated for features like inline functions can create minor performance overhead in performance-critical low-level code, compared to Java’s explicit primitive type system.
### Pros of Java (vs Kotlin)
1. **Unmatched maturity and backwards compatibility**: Java is one of the most stable production-grade languages ever built, with near-perfect backwards compatibility: code written for Java 1.0 (1996) will run on modern JVMs with minimal changes. Breaking changes between Java versions are extremely rare, making it ideal for long-lived enterprise systems.
2. **Larger ecosystem and talent pool**: Java boasts the largest JVM ecosystem, with battle-tested frameworks (Spring, Hibernate, Struts), debugging tools, and tutorials built for Java first. Hiring experienced Java developers is far cheaper and easier in most global regions than hiring senior Kotlin talent.
3. **Faster clean compilation**: As noted earlier, Java compiles full clean builds significantly faster than Kotlin, a major advantage for large teams with frequent CI/CD deployments.
4. **Simple, explicit type system**: Java’s type system has no "magic" features (e.g. no extension functions, no implicit type conversion) that can make Kotlin code flow hard to trace for large cross-functional teams. Java’s explicit primitive types also eliminate implicit boxing overhead for performance-critical code.
5. **Multi-vendor LTS support**: Enterprise teams can choose from multiple independent LTS providers for Java, with support timelines of up to 10+ years, reducing vendor lock-in and support costs for long-term systems.
### Cons of Java (vs Kotlin)
1. **Extreme verbosity and boilerplate**: Java requires hundreds of lines of redundant code for simple tasks like POJO creation, method overloading, and null checks, increasing development time, maintenance costs, and the risk of typos in boilerplate code.
2. **No built-in null safety**: NPEs remain the top cause of runtime crashes in Java applications, as the language does not enforce null checks at compile time. Java’s Optional utility is a partial workaround that is often misused or ignored.
3. **Slow-evolving async and functional support**: Java’s async programming tools (threads, `CompletableFuture`) are far more verbose and resource-heavy than Kotlin coroutines, and functional programming features (lambdas, streams) are limited and bolted on rather than natively integrated. New features like virtual threads and pattern matching take years to reach mainstream adoption due to Java’s slow LTS release cadence.
4. **No native cross-platform support**: Java can only run on platforms with a JVM, making it unsuitable for native iOS development or cross-platform mobile use cases that Kotlin Multiplatform supports.
5. **Limited modern language features**: While Java 17 added sealed classes, they are less flexible than Kotlin’s implementation, and Java has no equivalent for extension functions, default parameters, or smart casts, forcing developers to rely on messy utility classes and redundant explicit casting.
### Final Use Case Guidance
Choose Kotlin for Android development, cross-platform applications, modern backend microservices, and teams prioritizing developer velocity and reduced bug rates. Choose Java for long-lived legacy enterprise systems, performance-critical low-level code, and teams with large existing Java talent pools.

# Paper Outline: Mocha’s Unwritten History: Six Centuries of Yemeni Coffee from Sufi Zawiyas to Global Specialty Markets
## Abstract
This paper traces the 600-year history of Yemeni coffee, challenging dominant narratives that frame Yemen as a marginal, "forgotten" origin of global coffee. Drawing on Ottoman tax records, Sufi hagiographies, European mercantile correspondence, and ethnographic data from contemporary Yemeni smallholders, it argues that Yemeni coffee has been a core site of Yemeni political sovereignty, religious piety, social identity, and economic resistance across pre-modern, colonial, and contemporary eras. The paper further analyzes how 21st-century specialty coffee movements and ongoing civil conflict have reshaped Yemeni coffee’s global reputation and material conditions for producers.
### Keywords
Yemeni coffee, qahwa, Mocha trade, Sufi religious culture, terroir, colonial biopiracy, specialty coffee, Yemeni civil war, agrarian labor

---

*1.1 Correcting the Narrative: Yemeni Coffee as a Foundational, Not Marginal, Global Commodity*  
1.2 Research Gap: Existing coffee history scholarship centers European colonial trade and Ethiopian origins, erasing Yemeni agency in developing cultivation, consumption, and global trade norms  
*1.3 Methodological Framework: Centering Yemeni Primary Sources to Decenter Colonial Framings of Coffee History*  
1.4 Research Questions and Thesis Statement

*3.1 Rasulid Court Patronage of Coffee as a Symbol of Dynastic Legitimacy*

## 4.0 The Golden Age of Mocha: Ottoman Rule and Global Dominance, 1517–1839 CE
*4.1 Ottoman Administrative Policies and the State Monopoly on Yemeni Coffee Exports*  
*4.2 The Port of Mocha: From Regional Fishing Village to Global Coffee Emporium*

*7.4 Humanitarian Commodification: Fair Trade, Direct Trade, and Farmer Support Initiatives Amid Conflict*

## 8.0 Conclusion

8.3 Broader Implications: Centering Marginalized Origins in Global Commodity History

# The Aluminum Can: A Paradox of Food Access, Material Innovation, and Waste
On a rainy weekday evening, when the clock ticks past 7 p.m., backpacks are strewn across the entryway, and two hungry children are begging for dinner, millions of parents reach for the same quiet lifeline in their pantry: an aluminum can of chicken noodle soup, a can of steamed corn, and a can of baked beans, all coming together to make a quick, nourishing meal in less than 10 minutes. This mundane, universal moment is only possible because of the aluminum can, a food storage material that has reshaped how we preserve, access, and consume food over the last 70 years, while also presenting urgent, solvable challenges around global waste. Long before aluminum became a staple of pantry shelves, food storage was a labor-intensive, inconsistent practice limited by the materials available to households and food producers. For centuries, families relied on root cellars, salting, smoking, and jarring to keep food edible through harsh winters or poor harvests, but these methods only worked for certain foods and required constant upkeep to avoid spoilage. The first commercial food cans, introduced in the early 19th century, were made of tin-plated steel, a heavy, rust-prone material that required specialized tools to open and often left a metallic aftertaste on the food stored inside. It was not until the post-WWII economic boom, when aluminum manufacturing became scaled and affordable for consumer goods, that food producers began testing the metal as a superior alternative for food storage.

What makes aluminum such a revolutionary material for food storage is its unique combination of physical properties: it is lightweight, malleable enough to be pressed into thin, stackable cans, and 100% impermeable to light, oxygen, and moisture—the three main environmental factors that cause food to spoil. Unlike plastic storage containers, aluminum does not absorb food odors or stains, and it does not leach harmful chemicals into food when heated, as long as it is coated with the thin, food-safe lacquer that has been standard for food cans since the 1960s. This impermeability means that food stored in aluminum cans can stay shelf-stable for 2 to 5 years, and in some cases even longer, without the need for refrigeration or added artificial preservatives, a feat that no other widely available food storage material can match. For busy households, this shelf stability has transformed how we approach meal planning, allowing families to stock up on nutritious staples without worrying about them going bad before they can be used. Canned beans, canned tomatoes, canned fish, and pre-made canned meals like chili, macaroni and cheese, and vegetable stew cut down meal prep time from hours to minutes, making hot, balanced meals accessible to working parents, college students living in dorm rooms with mini-fridges, and people with disabilities that limit their ability to cook from scratch.

The value of aluminum canned food extends far beyond everyday convenience, however, as it is a critical resource for addressing food insecurity and supporting communities during crises. Food banks across the United States distribute more than 2 billion pounds of canned food annually, and aluminum cans are the preferred packaging for these donations because they are durable enough to survive transport across hundreds of miles, lightweight enough to keep shipping costs low, and unlikely to break or leak like glass jars or plastic containers. During the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns, when grocery stores faced shortages and millions of people lost access to consistent meals, sales of aluminum canned food surged by 30% as households stocked up on shelf-stable staples and relief organizations distributed millions of canned meals to newly unemployed families. Even in emergency situations like hurricane evacuations, earthquake relief efforts, and military deployments, aluminum canned meals are a non-negotiable staple, as they can be stored for years in extreme temperatures without spoiling and require no special preparation to eat. For outdoor enthusiasts, too, aluminum canned food is a go-to choice for multi-day camping trips or backpacking excursions, where refrigeration is unavailable and lightweight, easy-to-prepare meals are essential for sustaining energy.

For all its benefits as a food storage material and its role in expanding access to nutritious meals, however, the aluminum can is at the center of a growing global waste crisis that demands collective action. Aluminum is a uniquely recyclable material: it can be melted down and reshaped infinitely without losing any of its structural quality, and recycling a single aluminum can uses 95% less energy than producing a new can from raw bauxite ore. This means that a well-designed recycling system can almost eliminate the need for new aluminum production, cutting down on the millions of tons of toxic red mud waste generated by bauxite mining each year, a byproduct that can leach heavy metals into groundwater and destroy local ecosystems if not properly contained. Despite this enormous potential for circularity, only about 50% of aluminum food cans are recycled globally each year, which means millions of tons of valuable, infinitely reusable material end up as municipal waste in landfills or incinerators. There are many reasons for this low recycling rate: many consumers confuse aluminum food cans with steel cans and sort them incorrectly, or they leave leftover food residue in the cans, which can contaminate entire batches of recyclable material and lead recycling facilities to dump the whole load into general waste. Cans consumed on the go, at parks, concerts, or workplaces, are even less likely to be recycled, as public recycling bins are often scarce or mislabeled, leading to perfectly reusable aluminum cans being thrown into trash cans that end up in landfills. Unlike food waste, which decomposes in a matter of months, aluminum cans that end up in landfills do not biodegrade at all; they can remain fully intact for up to 500 years, taking up valuable landfill space and slowly leaching small amounts of chemicals from their food-safe lining into the surrounding soil over time. The rise of single-use convenience culture has exacerbated this waste problem, as more and more consumers opt for pre-portioned, single-serve canned meals instead of buying bulk ingredients and storing them in reusable containers, even though the aluminum material itself is recyclable.

Thankfully, there are a growing number of innovations and policy solutions that can reduce the waste associated with aluminum food cans while preserving their critical role in food storage and meal access. Material scientists have developed thinner aluminum can walls that use 30% less raw material than cans produced in the 1990s, cutting down on both production waste and the carbon footprint of each can without compromising its durability or ability to preserve food. Many regions have expanded their bottle bill programs, which add a small deposit to the cost of canned food and drinks that is refunded when consumers return the cans to designated collection points, a policy that has been shown to increase aluminum can recycling rates by up to 80% in areas where it is implemented. Some food brands are also experimenting with reusable aluminum can systems, where consumers can purchase meals in aluminum cans, return the cleaned cans to the brand or a participating grocery store, and have them refilled with fresh soup, stew, or other staples, eliminating single-use waste entirely. Community organizations have also stepped up, hosting can drives that not only collect canned meals for food-insecure families but also educate donors about the importance of rinsing cans before recycling to avoid contamination and reduce post-consumer waste. Even small, individual actions can make a meaningful difference: rinsing out an aluminum can after finishing a meal and placing it in a recycling bin ensures that the material can be reused for another can, a bicycle part, or even a construction material, keeping it out of landfills and reducing the need for new, waste-generating bauxite mining. In the end, the aluminum can is a paradox: it is a life-changing food storage material that has made nutritious meals accessible to millions of people who would otherwise struggle to put food on the table, but it also contributes to a global waste crisis when not managed through intentional, collective action. We cannot dismiss the value of aluminum cans for food storage, especially for vulnerable populations who rely on shelf-stable meals to get through times of crisis or financial hardship, but we also cannot ignore the urgent need to build more circular systems that minimize waste and maximize the potential of this infinitely reusable material. The next time you reach for an aluminum can in your pantry to make a quick weeknight meal, take a moment to appreciate the decades of innovation that went into that small, lightweight container, and then take the extra 10 seconds to rinse it out and recycle it, so that its material can continue to serve communities for generations to come.

Brilliant Le Hou is a leading figure in equitable climate adaptation and cross cultural community organizing rooted in the US Gulf Coast.

*Early Life and Formative Roots*
They were raised in a tight knit Vietnamese fishing community in Plaquemines Parish Louisiana after their parents resettled there as refugees in 1992. They spent much of their childhood helping their father and uncles mend nets and harvest oysters from local marshlands. They witnessed first hand the slow destruction of those marshes from sea level rise and unregulated industrial runoff. That loss drove their early interest in protecting the ecosystems that sustained their community. They attended Louisiana State University on a full scholarship for environmental science and worked part time at a neighborhood community garden to deliver free produce to elderly residents of nearby food deserts.

*Career Advancing Community Led Climate Solutions*
After graduating in 2015 they joined the Gulf Coast Center for Law & Policy as a climate resilience coordinator. They led a successful campaign to secure 20 million dollars in state funding for nature based flood protection projects in working class coastal parishes. They also launched a program to train youth from immigrant and Black and Indigenous communities of color to lead local climate advocacy efforts. The program has graduated over 120 young leaders who have gone on to pass local policies to expand public green space and affordable storm proof housing. In 2020 they left their policy role to launch a regional cooperative that supports small scale fishing families affected by coastal erosion and storm damage.

*Recognition and Long Term Vision*
In 2023 they received a MacArthur Fellowship for their innovative work centering marginalized communities in climate action. They are currently leading a multi state initiative to create permanent protected coastal land trusts for Indigenous and immigrant fishing communities across the US Gulf Coast. They also publish a monthly zine that shares traditional ecological knowledge from Gulf Coast communities with young climate activists across the country. They still live in Plaquemines Parish with their partner and two young children. They devote their free time to leading free wetland restoration workshops for local youth and families. Their work prioritizes mutual aid and community leadership over top down policy solutions that often leave the most vulnerable groups behind.

7-Day China Itinerary (Classic Cultural Route, ideal for first-time visitors):
Day 1: Arrival in Beijing. Morning: Arrive at Beijing Capital International Airport, transfer to downtown hotel, pick up a China SIM card or download a VPN for internet access. Afternoon: Explore Tiananmen Square, the world’s largest public square, then visit the Forbidden City (Palace Museum), the imperial palace of the Ming and Qing dynasties. Evening: Dinner at a local Peking duck restaurant in Wangfujing Street, walk along Wangfujing Snack Street for street food. Local Tip: Book Forbidden City tickets 7+ days in advance via the official Palace Museum website; tickets sell out fast.
Day 2: Beijing (Great Wall Day Trip). Morning: Early private transfer to Mutianyu Section of the Great Wall (1.5hr drive), less crowded than Badaling; take a cable car up to the wall for panoramic views. Afternoon: Hike 2-3km along the wall, explore the watchtowers, take the toboggan slide down for a fun experience. Afternoon: Stop at the Ming Tombs, the burial site of 13 Ming dynasty emperors, on the way back to Beijing. Evening: Dinner at a traditional courtyard restaurant in the Hutongs. Local Tip: Wear comfortable hiking shoes and bring sunscreen and water for the Great Wall hike.
Day 3: Beijing Cultural Exploration. Morning: Explore the Lama Temple (Yonghegong), the largest Tibetan Buddhist temple outside Tibet, then wander through the nearby Nanluoguxiang Hutong, a historic alleyway with cafes, boutiques, and courtyard homes. Afternoon: Visit the Summer Palace, a vast imperial garden with a lake and traditional pavilions. Evening: Attend a Peking Opera performance at the Liyuan Theatre, dinner with dumplings at a local family-run restaurant. Local Tip: Rent a bicycle to explore the Hutongs for a more authentic experience.
Day 4: Beijing → Xi’an (High-Speed Rail). Morning: Take the 4.5hr high-speed rail from Beijing West Station to Xi’an, the ancient capital of 13 Chinese dynasties. Afternoon: Check into Xi’an hotel, explore the Xi’an City Wall, one of the best-preserved ancient city walls in the world; rent a bicycle to cycle along the 14km wall. Evening: Dinner at the Muslim Quarter, a vibrant bazaar with Uyghur and Hui cuisine, try roujiamo (Chinese hamburger) and biangbiang noodles. Local Tip: Download Alipay or WeChat Pay for cashless transactions, which are standard across China.
Day 5: Xi’an (Terracotta Warriors Day Trip). Morning: Early visit to the Terracotta Army Museum (1hr drive from downtown), a UNESCO site with thousands of life-sized terracotta soldiers built for Emperor Qin Shi Huang’s tomb. Afternoon: Explore the three pits of the museum, visit the Qin Shi Huang Mausoleum Site Park nearby. Evening: Watch the Tang Dynasty Music and Dance Show, a performance showcasing Tang dynasty art and culture, followed by a traditional dinner. Local Tip: Hire a licensed guide at the museum to learn the history of the Terracotta Warriors; audio guides are also available in multiple languages.
Day 6: Xi’an Leisure & Day Excursion. Morning: Visit the Big Wild Goose Pagoda, a 7th-century Buddhist pagoda built to house Buddhist scriptures brought from India by Xuanzang. Afternoon: Optional day trip to Huaqing Hot Springs, a imperial retreat with natural hot springs and historical sites, or spend the afternoon shopping for souvenirs in Xi’an’s Old Town. Evening: Attend the Grand Tang Mall light show, a free nightly show with traditional music and light projections. Local Tip: Avoid buying overpriced souvenirs near the Terracotta Army Museum; shop in Xi’an’s Old Town for better prices.
Day 7: Xi’an → Departure (or Extension to Shanghai). Morning: Private transfer to Xi’an Xianyang International Airport for departure, or take a 2hr high-speed rail to Shanghai for an extended trip. Afternoon: Optional last-minute sightseeing or souvenir shopping in Xi’an’s Muslim Quarter. Evening: Arrive at the airport for international departure. Local Tip: Arrive at the airport 3 hours before international flights to allow for security checks.

My planned perfect Saturday was toast – until I remembered the crumpled [annual family membership pass] to Ripley’s Aquarium tucked in the back of my wallet, a Christmas gift from my sister that I’d written off as “for people who actually have children.”

I grinned. Turns out, Ripley’s isn’t just for 3rd grade field trips – it’s for anyone who needs a little low-stakes magic on a crummy day.

Most visitors rush through the jellyfish gallery to get to the penguin exhibit, and I get it – baby penguins waddling around are very cute. But if you linger 10 extra minutes, you’ll spot a tiny, easy-to-miss sign tucked by the moon jelly tank advertising [glow-in-the-dark jellyfish yoga], a weekly Wednesday evening event for adults only. I signed up for the next class on a whim, and y’all – it’s the most chaotic, peaceful self-care activity I’ve ever tried. The gallery lights are dimmed so the jellyfish’s neon pink and blue tentacles glow like floating lanterns, the instructor plays lo-fi sea shanty remixes (yes, that’s a thing), and no one judges you if you pause mid-downward dog to film a jellyfish doing a little spin mid-float. After class, everyone gets a free cup of sea salt lemonade and exclusive access to the touch pool without the crowds of tiny hands grabbing at the stingrays.

Let’s talk about the elephant in every attraction: overpriced, mid food. It’s the best $6 I’ve spent all month – and way better than the crumbly granola bar I forgot to eat until I got home.

I got to hold one of the palm-sized baby turtles (supervised, don’t worry – no unauthorized turtle snuggling allowed) and left with a waterproof sticker that says “I <3 Sea Turtles” that’s now plastered on my laptop. It’s so refreshing to visit an attraction that actually gives back to the ecosystem it showcases.

I went last week with my roommate, and we have a very dramatic photo of us pretending to outswim a great white that’s now taped front and center on our fridge.

Pro tip: If you go on [weekday afternoons after 3 p.m.], tickets are 20% off, and most of the field trip groups have already loaded back onto their buses for the day, so you can wander the exhibits in relative peace, no tiny humans cutting you off to get a better look at the octopus.

I used to write off Ripley’s Aquarium as a cheesy, kid-only tourist spot, but now it’s my go-to for rainy days, bad first date do-overs, and even just midweek mental health breaks when I need to step away from my work laptop and stare at fish for an hour. Whether you’re a local looking for a low-stakes adventure or a tourist visiting [coastal home city] for the first time, do yourself a favor and skip the overcrowded boardwalk (or the rained-out hike) and spend a few hours at Ripley’s. - **Sparkling Coffee Toast**: Attendees raise flutes of *Java Sparkling Wine* (fermented from Java Island coffee cherries) to the “Brewmaster Grand Champion” (highest combined score on escape room + certification questions).

1. **Java Brewmaster’s Vault**: Private digital access to exclusive content: Gosling’s uncut 1995 demo, Spring Boot Core Team’s internal design docs, and a JVM tuning cheat sheet hand-signed by 10 Java Champions.

The first and most important step before spending any money on your business is validating that there are actual customers willing to pay for what you plan to offer. Too many new owners sink thousands of dollars into inventory, custom websites, or branding work before ever speaking to a potential customer outside their friend group, leading to wasted resources and failed launches. *Prioritize problem validation over product building in your first 90 days*. To do this, connect with at least 20 people who fit your target customer profile (for example, local apartment dwellers with small dogs, if you’re considering pet care services) and ask specific questions: what similar solutions have they paid for in the past? What frustrates them most about those options? What price point would feel like a good value for a fix? If 15 or more of those people say they would pay your proposed price for your solution, you have a viable foundation to build on.
***
Once you’ve validated your core idea, build your financial foundation to avoid common cash flow crunches that sink 82% of new small businesses, per U.S. Small Business Administration data. *Open a dedicated business bank account and set aside 30% of every revenue dollar for taxes and unexpected costs*, even if you’re operating as a sole proprietorship with no plans to hire staff in the near future. Mixing personal and business funds leads to messy bookkeeping, missed tax deductions, and potential IRS penalties, while the 30% rule covers self-employment taxes, unexpected permit fees, equipment repairs, and slow seasonal lulls. Avoid high-interest personal loans to fund your launch whenever possible; use personal savings, or a 0% APR business credit card that you pay off in full each month, if you need short-term capital for supplies or marketing. Before quitting your full-time job, build a 3-month buffer for both your personal living expenses and business operating costs, so you don’t have to rely on projected revenue to cover basic needs in your first year.
***
When you start making sales, resist the urge to pour your entire marketing budget into chasing new customers, and focus equally on retaining the buyers you already have. *Your repeat customers will drive 70% of your long-term revenue, so build loyalty from the first interaction*. Repeat customers spend an average of 67% more than first-time buyers, and their word-of-mouth recommendations are free, high-converting marketing that performs better than paid social ads for most small, local or niche businesses. Small, personal touches go a long way: if you run a mobile car detailing service, leave a branded air freshener and a handwritten note with a 15% off code for a follow-up wash after every appointment. If you sell handmade home goods online, send a personalized email 10 days after delivery to check in on their order, and invite them to join a text list for exclusive restock alerts and loyalty discounts. Even for service-based businesses like virtual administrative support, checking in with clients quarterly to ask how you can better support their goals builds long-term retention.
***
Don’t skip the seemingly boring regulatory and operational prep work that acts as a safety net for your business. Even home-based, part-time operations need to comply with local rules: for example, a home bakery will almost always require a cottage food license, regular health inspections, and clear allergen labeling on all products, even if you only sell through social media. General liability insurance costs less than $30 a month for most small service or product businesses, and can save you tens of thousands of dollars if a client sues over property damage, injury, or a missed deadline that costs them revenue. Create clear, written policies for core operations before you get busy: outline your customer response time, refund policy, and core work hours, so you don’t make ad-hoc decisions that lead to inconsistent service or personal burnout. Taking a weekend to map out these rules and check off all local regulatory requirements will prevent costly surprises down the line.
***
Finally, build your business to fit your life, not the other way around, to avoid the burnout that causes 30% of new small business owners to close their doors within two years. It’s easy to fall into the trap of working 12-hour days, answering customer inquiries at 10 p.m., and accepting every client request that comes in, especially when you’re excited to grow. But overworking leads to sloppy service, resentment, and poor decision-making long before you hit your revenue goals. Set clear boundaries early: stick to your posted work hours, turn off work notifications outside of those times, and raise your prices as demand increases instead of taking on more work than you can comfortably handle. Sustainable, slow growth is far more stable than rapid, unplanned growth: it’s better to have 10 happy, high-paying clients that let you work 40 hours a week than 30 low-paying clients that leave you too exhausted to provide good service or enjoy the freedom of running your own business.

the undergrowth grabs at boot cuffs as the four of them move single file through the gash of unmarked sector 7, the only light the thin spill of distant starlight sifting through thorn thickets. rusted plows and half-collapsed barns dot the fallow fields, left behind when families fled the border closure three years prior, their wood slats warped, their tin roofs pocked with bullet holes from random patrol skirmishes. moth, point, holds up a fist before anyone steps over a half-buried tripwire strung between two gnarled oak saplings, her free hand flicking a signal back to rook, tern, kite, the rest of the team freezing mid-step, breath fogging thin in the cool air. this is the hour where even the border hounds curl deep into their straw bedding, where farmhouses ten klicks out have long snuffed their lantern wicks, where the only sound before the tripwire was the soft hoot of a scops owl drifting over the rows of overgrown corn.

rook’s palms slick on the polymer rail of his rifle. it’s his first time across the demarcation line, his first op off the training ranges, and he’d forgotten how heavy gear gets when you have to carry it for three klicks through brambles that snag at your ammo pouches and leave thin, stinging cuts across your wrists. moth had told him before they moved out that the worst part of this work is the waiting, the quiet that settles so deep you start to hear your own pulse thudding in your ears, and he’d thought she was being dramatic until ten minutes ago, when a fox had darted out from a hedge and he’d almost squeezed the trigger before tern’s hand clamped down on his barrel, hard enough to leave a bruise.

they reach the derelict pumping station ten minutes later, its concrete walls crumbled at the corners, rebar sticking out like twisted twigs, a rusted chain slung across the gap where the front door used to hang. moth signals for kite to take overwatch in the oak at the edge of the clearing, tern to cover the south approach, then motions for rook to follow her through the gap, their boots crunching over shards of broken glass and old beer cans left by teens who snuck out here years ago, before the border was sealed, before the sensors went up.

the contact is huddled behind the main pump, her jacket pulled up over her head, a canvas bag slung over her shoulder, her eyes wide when she sees moth’s faint glow stick signal, the prearranged pattern of two quick flashes, one long. she’s a civil engineer, employed by the occupying force to lay the new sensor lines across the sector, and she’s been leaking intel for six months, ever since her brother was picked up at a checkpoint and never brought home. she pulls a ruggedized data drive from the lining of her jacket, presses it into moth’s palm, her fingers cold, her voice so quiet it’s almost a whisper, says they moved up the installation timeline, that the sensors will go live at first light, that if they don’t get the data back to command before then, every village within twenty klicks will be cut off from supply routes, from the medical convoys that come through once a month.

moth tucks the drive into the waterproof pouch sewn into the inside of her vest, nods, motions for the contact to follow them, when they hear it, the low rumble of a patrol truck coming down the dirt road that runs past the pumping station, tires crunching over crushed limestone. kite’s voice comes over the comms, thin and tight, says two trucks, four personnel each, spotlight sweeping the west field, heading straight for the clearing.

they huddle down behind the pump, rook pressing his back to the cold concrete, his breath caught in his throat, as the first truck pulls into the clearing, its spotlight sweeping over the walls, over the hedge line, over the oak where kite is perched, hidden in the thick leaves. the spotlight pauses for a long, stretched second on the gap where the door used to be, and rook’s finger tenses on the trigger, before the spotlight swings away, moving toward the south field, where tern is pressed into a ditch, half covered in fallen leaves. one of the patrol members calls out something in a language rook doesn’t speak, loud and rough, and there’s the sound of a beer can cracking open, of laughter, before the trucks rumble away again, heading toward the border outpost three klicks east.

they wait another twenty minutes before moving, just to be sure, no one speaking, no one moving more than to shift their weight to take pressure off a sore ankle. kite drops down from the oak first, gives the all clear, then tern comes up from the south ditch, leaves stuck in her hair, a thorn stuck in her cheek that she pulls out without flinching. they move out again, single file, the contact between rook and tern, moth leading, kite bringing up the rear, moving faster now, the drive heavy in moth’s vest, the knowledge that they have three hours until first light pushing them forward, their boots barely making a sound on the soft dirt of the trail.

they cross back over the demarcation line an hour later, the staging tent glowing faint behind a screen of pine trees, the extraction team waiting with hot tea and dry blankets for the contact. moth pulls the drive from her pouch, hands it to the intel officer who steps forward to meet them, and for a second, no one says anything, just breathes, the cool air sharp in their lungs, the first pale pink tint starting to bleed into the edge of the sky. rook leans against a pine tree, sets his rifle down, wipes the sweat from his forehead, and moth claps him on the shoulder, gives him a rare, half smile, says he did good, that he didn’t freeze when the spotlight hit, that he’s got the hang of this.

he nods, looks out over the sector they just crossed, the thorn thickets, the derelict pumping station, the distant border outpost, and thinks about the villages, the medical convoys, the engineer’s brother, and for the first time since he signed up, he doesn’t feel like he’s just playing at this, doesn’t feel like a kid in a uniform with a rifle. he feels like he did something that matters.

# The Unseen Reality of Disability: Beyond Tragedy and Inspiration Porn

The oat milk latte slips from Mia’s grip before she can register the twinge in her hypermobile wrist, splattering across the sidewalk outside her neighborhood coffee shop. The stranger who stops to stare doesn’t hand her a napkin, or ask if she’s hurt. They just tilt their head, voice soft with a pity that curdles in Mia’s chest, and say, “Wow, you’re so brave for being out here.”

Mia, 28, has Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a connective tissue disorder that causes chronic pain, joint dislocations, and frequent fatigue. She is not brave for running errands on a Tuesday. She is annoyed that her $7 latte is gone, that her wrist will ache for the next three hours, that a stranger has turned a mundane, frustrating moment into a testament of her supposed heroism.

This is the first and most persistent gap between public perception of disability and its reality: for most abled people, disability is either a tragic, life-ending sentence, or a feel-good plot device for viral reels and motivational speeches. For the 1 in 4 adults in the U.S. who live with a disability, it is mostly just… life. It is the 20 extra minutes budgeted every morning for physical therapy before logging into work. It is the 12th restaurant you cross off your friends’ dinner list because its only entrance is a flight of stairs. It is the quiet math of spoon theory, tallying energy like loose change to make sure you have enough left to brush your teeth after a grocery run. It is boring, and messy, and ordinary, in the same way any life is ordinary.

Too often, disability is framed as a personal flaw, a problem to be fixed or overcome by individual grit. But the core truth of disabled life, articulated decades ago by disabled activists in the U.S. and UK, is that disability is not created by a person’s body or mind—it is created by a world built for a narrow, fictional idea of “normal.” A wheelchair user is not disabled by their inability to climb stairs; they are disabled by the absence of ramps, elevators, and curb cuts. A Deaf person is not disabled by their inability to hear; they are disabled by the lack of sign language interpreters, captioned media, and workplaces that refuse to accommodate their communication needs. An autistic person is not disabled by their sensory needs; they are disabled by loud, overstimulating public spaces and a culture that punishes stimming and non-neurotypical social cues as “rude.”

This reality is made even more invisible by the fact that most disabilities are not visible. Javi, 34, lives with complex PTSD and fibromyalgia, and uses a lightweight mobility scooter to conserve energy and avoid the overstimulation that comes with standing in crowded lines. Twice in the last month, strangers have yelled at him for “faking” a disability, pointing out that he stood up to reach a bottle of soda at the grocery store. For invisible disabled people, ableism often comes in the form of constant, exhausting gatekeeping: having to prove your pain is real, your fatigue is not just laziness, your need for accommodation is not a ploy to get special treatment. There is no universal face of disability, no checklist of symptoms or visible aids that make someone “truly” disabled. Disability can be permanent or temporary, static or fluctuating; anyone could join the community at any time, a truth most abled people spend their lives avoiding. It is an identity as diverse as humanity itself, encompassing physical disabilities, neurodivergence, chronic illness, mental health conditions, and hundreds of other experiences that rarely fit the abled public’s narrow idea of what disability looks like.

Of course, the reality of disability is not just mundane frustration and systemic barriers. There is a joy in disabled community that abled people rarely see: the group chat where friends share hacks for supportive shoes that don’t look like medical equipment, the mutual aid funds that raise money for wheelchairs and rent when insurance refuses to cover care, the weekly game nights where no one blinks if someone has to leave mid-round because of a migraine, or stims loudly during a tense game of Codenames, or needs to take a 20-minute nap on the couch halfway through. Disabled people have built cultures of care and solidarity that prioritize people over productivity, that recognize rest as a right, that celebrate the small, creative ways we adapt to a world that was not built for us. That joy is as much a part of disabled reality as the ableism we face.

The greatest disservice abled culture does to disabled people is reducing our lives to lessons for abled people. We are not here to teach you gratitude, or resilience, or to make you feel better about your own lives. We are here to live ours, the same as anyone else: to fall in love, to burn toast, to get bad haircuts, to complain about our bosses, to celebrate birthdays, to grieve losses. The only “lesson” disability offers is that the world could be kinder, more accessible, more generous, if we stopped building it for only one kind of person. It offers the truth that diversity is not a buzzword, but a basic fact of human life, and that access and care are collective responsibilities, not individual burdens.

Next time you see a disabled person drop their coffee, hand them a napkin instead of calling them brave. Advocate for ramps in your local library, for captions on your company’s Zoom calls, for disabled candidates running for office. Listen when disabled people tell you what they need, instead of assuming you know better. Is there anything else I can help with?

# I Rode Public Transit For 12 Years, And These 3 Wild Moments Beat Any Curated Trip I’ve Ever Paid For
If you’ve ever complained about a delayed train, a seat that’s just a little too sticky, or a stranger’s very loud personal phone call, I get it. Public transit gets a bad rap as a tedious, utilitarian means to an end—something to endure while scrolling TikTok until you reach your stop. But after a decade plus of relying on buses, trains, streetcars, and even the occasional converted school bus to get everywhere from job interviews to backpacking day trips, I’ve collected a list of wild, warm, and deeply weird moments that beat any first-class flight or curated road trip I’ve ever booked. Here are the top three that still make me smile:

## Ridden: The Portland MAX Cat Café Car (2019)
I was 26, stressed out of my mind for a marketing job interview, wearing a blazer that was too tight, and running two minutes late when I hopped the Blue Line without glancing at the car number. The doors slid open and instead of the usual scuffed plastic seats and faint smell of burnt coffee, I was hit with lavender air freshener, soft indie folk, and a purr so loud it sounded like a small generator.
The entire car had been gutted and refitted for a local animal shelter’s “Ride & Purr” fundraiser: low pile carpet, wall-mounted cat trees, string lights, and 12 adoptable kitties wandering between commuters’ laps. Volunteers handed out mini oat milk lattes and little printed cards with each cat’s bio. I plopped down next to a chonky orange tabby named Cheeto, whose bio said he loved “napping on laptops and stealing french fries,” and he immediately curled up on my blazer, purring so hard my shoulder vibrated.
I missed my stop by three stations, showed up to my interview 20 minutes late covered in orange cat hair, and still got the job. The best part? I followed the shelter’s Instagram later that week and saw Cheeto had been adopted by a college student who’d ridden the same car that day, too.

## Seen: The NYC A Train Gospel Pop-Up (2022)
I was in New York visiting my sister, coming home from a late dinner in Brooklyn, crammed into a rush-hour A train so packed I could barely lift my phone to text her I was on my way. At 59th Street, a group of four women in their 70s, all wearing matching sequined church hats and glittery tote bags, squeezed on, one toting a tiny portable speaker slung over her arm.
No announcement, no fanfare—they just locked eyes, nodded, and started singing a gospel rendition of “Amazing Grace” in four-part harmony so crisp it cut straight through the rumble of the train. At first, people stared, then pulled out their headphones, then started humming along. Halfway through the second verse, one of the women pulled a crumpled Ziploc bag out of her tote and passed it around, yelling over the train noise, “No tips, y’all—we take prayer requests! Write ‘em down, we’ll lift ‘em up at service this week.”
People scribbled on receipts, napkins, the back of work memos; a 10-year-old kid drew a stick figure of his golden retriever, who he wrote was “at the vet for his tummy.” By the time they got off at 125th Street, the whole car was cheering, a guy who’d been scowling at his laptop the whole ride was wiping his eyes, and someone passed around a pack of mint gum like we were all old friends at a cookout.

## Ridden: The Oaxacan Camioneta With a Rooster Co-Pilot (2021)
I was backpacking through Oaxaca, trying to get from the tiny mountain pueblo of San José del Pacífico to Puerto Escondido, and the only public transit option was a camioneta—an old school bus converted into a rural local bus—that ran “whenever we have enough people,” per the hand-scrawled sign taped to the side of the town’s only taco stand.
When it pulled up, it was neon pink, covered in hand-painted murals of Frida Kahlo and palm trees, strung with fairy lights that blinked even in the daytime, and had a rooster in a tiny leather harness perched on the dashboard next to the driver. The driver, Pancho, introduced the rooster as Pancho Jr., his “official ticket checker and first mate.”
Pancho Jr. didn’t crow the whole ride—he just napped on the dashboard, occasionally tilting his head to watch people haul sacks of corn or bunches of bananas onto the bus. Pancho didn’t follow a set schedule or even a set route: he stopped to pick up an abuela walking two miles to the next town with her granddaughter, pulled over halfway so we could all pick mangoes from a wild tree on the side of the road, and blared Vicente Fernández so loud the windows rattled. The ride took three hours longer than Google Maps said it would, and I wouldn’t have cut a single minute of it.

Here’s the thing about public transit that no one tells you: it’s the only shared public space left where you don’t get to curate who you’re around. You can’t filter out the shelter team that turns a train into a cat café, or the group of women who turn a miserable rush hour into a church service, or the bus driver who brings his rooster to work. Those moments are messy, unplanned, and way more interesting than any algorithm-curated experience you could pay for.
I still take Uber sometimes, when I’m running late or it’s pouring rain. But I’ll always choose the bus or the train first, just in case Cheeto the tabby or Pancho Jr. the rooster is along for the ride.

P.S. If you ever see a guy carrying a cat hair-covered blazer on the Portland MAX? That’s probably me. Say hi.

### Pros and Cons of Using Two Different Names for the Same Thing
Using two distinct names for the same denotative thing—meaning the pair function as tight, contextually interchangeable synonyms—carries distinct benefits and drawbacks, shaped by the setting in which the synonyms are used. While many languages have large sets of synonyms for common concepts, limiting a referent to just two paired synonyms balances flexibility and standardization, but the tradeoffs remain significant. Below is a structured breakdown, with explicit focus on how synonyms shape communication, learning, and collaboration:

---

#### Pros
1. **Targeted Audience Alignment**  
Tight synonyms for the same core concept let communicators tailor language to an audience’s expertise, cultural background, or identity without altering the subject of discussion. For example, the synonyms “autistic person” and “person with autism” refer to the exact same neurotype, but these synonyms align with different community preferences: many self-advocates prefer identity-first language (“autistic person”), while older clinical frameworks often use person-first language (“person with autism”). Having both synonyms available lets speakers signal respect for a group’s preferred framing without needing to explain a new, unfamiliar term.
2. **Rhetorical and Creative Flexibility**  
For writers, public speakers, and storytellers, having access to paired synonyms for the same thing eliminates awkward, distracting repetition and lets creators craft more rhythmic, engaging work. A middle school English teacher, for instance, might encourage students to alternate between the synonyms “joyful” and “elated” when describing a character’s mood, as these synonyms carry nearly identical denotations for young readers but prevent the prose from feeling flat or repetitive. This flexibility is a core reason languages naturally accumulate synonyms over time, as speakers seek variety without shifting the core meaning of their message.
3. **Reduced Friction Across Siloed Groups**  
In cross-sector collaboration, synonyms that are standard in different fields let teams recognize shared priorities without requiring full retraining in each group’s jargon. For example, urban planners use the term “active transportation” while public health researchers use the term “human-powered mobility” to refer to the exact same set of travel modes (walking, biking, skateboarding, etc.). These synonyms let both groups retain their field’s standard terminology while quickly recognizing they are discussing the same policy goal, eliminating the need for burdensome jargon translation during cross-sector meetings.

---

#### Cons
1. **Increased Cognitive Load for Novices and Language Learners**  
For people new to a language, field, or community, paired synonyms for the same core concept add unnecessary work to master basic vocabulary, as they must memorize twice as many terms for identical referents. For example, a first-year nursing student might be confused when their rotation supervisor uses the synonyms “hypertension” and “high blood pressure” interchangeably without clarifying they mean the same thing; these unacknowledged synonyms can lead to medical charting errors, misplaced confusion about core patient needs, and frustration that discourages new clinicians from staying in the field. Even intermediate English as a Second Language (ESL) learners often cite the sheer volume of synonyms as one of the most challenging parts of achieving fluency, as they cannot always tell when two terms are fully interchangeable versus when they carry subtle, unspoken connotations.
2. **Risk of Costly Misinterpretation in Regulated or Formal Contexts**  
In legal contracts, technical manuals, clinical guidelines, or regulatory documents, unstandardized synonyms for the same core thing can lead to dangerous, expensive misinterpretation. For example, if a construction contract uses the synonyms “load-bearing wall” and “structural wall” without explicitly defining them as interchangeable, a subcontractor might mistakenly modify a wall they do not recognize as critical, leading to structural damage, project delays, and costly legal battles. Regulated industries often spend tens of thousands of dollars annually creating official style guides that explicitly state which synonyms are interchangeable, an administrative overhead that would not exist if a single standardized term was used exclusively for core concepts.
3. **Artificial Perceptual Distinction Between Identical Concepts**  
When two synonyms are used consistently in separate silos, stakeholders can come to believe the synonyms refer to distinct things, creating unnecessary divides between groups working toward the same goal. WORD ASSOCIATIONS paid off in the end
