Poem 1
I grew up on the rule of brown:
no streaks, no bleach, no anything
that might make the world look twice
at the girl who was supposed to be soft,
unobtrusive, easy to forget.
So at 27, when I squeezed the neon peach dye
into the dented plastic bowl, latex gloves sticking
to the sweet, chemical tang of it,
my hands shook like I was stealing something holy.
It was 2 a.m., the radio humming 2000s pop
so loud the neighbors wouldn’t hear me sing off-key,
the bathroom mirror fogged with the heat of the shower
I’d run to steam the color into my roots,
that tingle on my scalp sharp as a secret,
like my head was finally catching up
to the bright thing I’d been carrying in my chest all these years.
I rinsed it out leaning over the tub,
water running tangerine down the drain
like I was washing out every quiet “don’t stand out”
my mother ever whispered while brushing my hair flat for school.
When I flipped my head up, blow dryer roaring,
and caught my reflection in the fogged glass,
I barely recognized her: cheeks flushed,
hair glowing like the inside of a sunset,
like someone had reached into the sky
and pulled the last soft hour of summer
straight into my follicles.
The next day, a little girl in the cereal aisle
tugged her mom’s sleeve and pointed,
“Her hair looks like popsicle juice,”
and when her mom flushed and apologized for the rudeness,
I twisted a strand between my fingers and grinned,
said “It tastes like it too, if you ask me.”
The barista wrote “peach hair” on my latte cup
in sparkly gel pen. When a summer rain caught me
walking home, my hair stuck to my neck in streaks,
and I knelt to catch my reflection in a puddle,
and for the first time in my life,
I didn’t look away.
I still have the stains: a faint orange smudge
on the collar of my favorite white tee,
a ring around the shower tile that won’t scrub away,
a peach smudge on the edge of my pillowcase
where I rest my head at night.
They’re not messes. They’re proof I got to choose
to be bright, to be loud, to be something
someone might point at and smile at,
proof I got to make myself look like the joy
I spent so long hiding inside.
******
Poem 2
Dyed hair is not a one-time joy. It’s a cycle,
a ritual, a love letter I rewrite to myself
every three months, when the roots grow in
and the color fades soft at the ends, worn thin
by sun and shampoo and the way I twist strands
when I’m nervous, when I’m giddy, when I’m thinking
of what color to try next.
It was lavender first, mixed in my best friend’s kitchen,
three bottles of cheap semi-permanent dye,
lo mein containers scattered across the linoleum,
her tabby cat curling up on the old towel we laid out
like he knew we were making magic.
It didn’t stay bright lavender for long:
first it faded to cotton candy pink at the ends,
then to silver lilac, then to a pale, milky white
that glowed in the dark of movie theaters,
that looked like stardust when I walked under streetlights
on my way home from late shifts.
I loved every stage, not just the first bold burst,
loved the way it changed with me, slow,
like the seasons turning, no pressure to stay the same.
Next it was forest green, for October,
dyed while I listened to spooky true-crime podcasts,
the house smelling like cinnamon and simmering apple cider.
It blended with the pine needles when I hiked,
matched the moss on the oak trees behind my apartment,
and a little old lady on the trail stopped me
and said “you look like a tree nymph, dear,”
and I carried that compliment with me for weeks,
tucked into the strands like a leaf I’d picked and saved.
People love to say you’re too old for it,
too professional, too much of a grown-up
to walk around with hair that doesn’t grow
out of your head that way, as if joy
has an age limit, as if grown-ups don’t deserve
to decorate their bodies like the temples they are.
They don’t know about the quiet joy of it:
running your hands through freshly dyed hair
while you make coffee in the morning,
the soft color bleeding a little into the shower water
like a watercolor painting, the way you catch
your reflection in a store window and do a double-take,
giddy all over again that this bright thing is yours.
They don’t know about the community:
the woman with electric blue hair at the grocery store
who winks at you across the tomato display,
the teen with neon pink bangs who high-fives you
at the punk show, the stranger with half-black half-white hair
who stops you on the street to ask what dye you used,
like you’re both part of a secret club
where the only membership requirement
is choosing to make yourself happy,
no apologies.
This winter I dyed it rose pink, soft as crushed velvet,
and when I walk through the snow,
the color glows like I’m carrying a little bit of summer
on my head, even when the wind cuts through my coat.
Last week I sent a selfie to my 16-year-old cousin,
who just dyed her hair electric teal after months
of begging her parents for permission,
and she texted back “we look like the main characters
of the fairy tale we get to write.”
She’s right. Dyed hair isn’t just color.
It’s the right to be your own work of art,
to reinvent yourself whenever you want,
to carry joy on your head, bright and unapologetic,
for everyone to see, for you to see,
every single time you look in the mirror.

SRE는 이렇게 정립한 지표와 목표를 기반으로 서비스 신뢰성 관리(management)를 체계적으로 수행한다. 장애가 발생하기 전 잠재적 위험 요소를 사전에 탐지해 개선하고, 장애 발생 시 신속한 원인 파악과 복구를 지원하며, 반복적으로 발생하는 운영 업무는 자동화 도구를 통해 효율화함으로써 서비스의 품질을 지속적으로 향상시키는 것이 SRE의 핵심 역할이다.

- No early alarms set for the next day!

Day 2: North Shore Public Transit Day Trip
- Wake up at 9am, grab a $3 iced coffee and plain malasada from a nearby food cart
- Buy a $3 day pass for TheBus (Oahu’s public transit, direct to North Shore in 1 hour)
- Stops: Dole Plantation for $5 pineapple whip, Waimea Bay for free cliff jumping (popular with local college students), and Pipeline Beach for photos
- Lunch: $12 garlic shrimp plate from Giovanni’s Shrimp Truck (10% student discount with ID)
- Evening: Bring your own snacks and soda for a free group bonfire at Sunset Beach (check local fire restrictions first)
- Bus back to Waikiki by 10pm

Day 3: Hike & Insta-Worthy East Oahu Day
- Wake up at 8am, pack snacks bought during a $10 total group Walmart run the night before
- Hike Manoa Falls (1 mile round-trip, easy, lush Jurassic Park filming spot, free entry) then Lanikai Pillboxes (2 mile round-trip, moderate, panoramic views of the Mokulua Islands, free entry)
- Midday: Swim at Lanikai Beach (consistently ranked one of the best beaches in the U.S., no entry fee)
- Lunch: $11 ahi poke bowl from Kailua Town’s Foodland Farms (student discount)
- Evening: Free outdoor movie at Waikiki Beach Walk (7pm, bring a blanket; screening of *Lilo & Stitch* for college night)

Day 4: Pearl Harbor & Souvenir Swap Meet
- Wake up at 8am, use pre-reserved free tickets for the USS Arizona Memorial (book 2 weeks in advance, no entry cost)
- Take TheBus to Pearl Harbor, spend 2 hours exploring the memorial and free visitor center exhibits
- Head next to the Aloha Stadium Swap Meet (open Wed, Sat, Sun, $1 entry) for cheap souvenirs: $5 flower leis, $10 custom surf keychains, $8 hand-printed t-shirts
- Lunch: $8 mix plate from local chain Zippy’s (student discount on all plate lunches)
- Evening: Trivia night at Waikiki Beach Hostel’s bar ($5 entry per team, top team wins a $50 bar tab to split)

Day 5: Hanauma Bay Snorkel & Waimanalo Beach Potluck
- Wake up at 9am, use $15 snorkel gear bought at Walmart (cheaper than renting)
- Head to Hanauma Bay Nature Preserve (student entry $15, reserve tickets 2 weeks in advance) for 3 hours of snorkeling with tropical fish and sea turtles
- Stop at Halona Blowhole (free entry) on the way out for photos
- Lunch: $10 coconut shrimp plate from a roadside Waimanalo food truck
- Evening: Group potluck at Waimanalo Beach (less crowded than Waikiki, free entry) – everyone brings a $5 snack (chips, fruit, soda) and grills $1 hot dogs from the Walmart run. End the night stargazing with no city light pollution.

Day 6: Community Luau & Waikiki Night Market
- Wake up at 10am, lazy beach morning to recharge
- Lunch: $8 spam sliders from a local food truck
- Head to the Waianae Community Luau (30 mins from Waikiki via TheBus, $35 per person student rate – 70% cheaper than resort luaus) – includes all-you-can-eat kalua pork, lomi lomi salmon, and haupia, plus local hula and fire knife performances
- Evening: Walk the Waikiki Night Market (open 5-10pm Fri/Sat, free entry) for $3 mango sticky rice, live reggae music, and $10 handmade jewelry
- Late night: Tiki bar crawl with hostel friends – most nearby bars offer $5 mai tai specials for students with ID

Day 7: Departure & Last-Minute Grindz
- Sleep in until 10am, no alarms
- Squeeze in 1 last hour of beach time in Waikiki, grab a $5 shave ice from Matsumoto’s kiosk on the way back
- Pack up and check out of the hostel
- Stop at Leonard’s Malasadas near the airport for a $3 bag of warm malasadas to bring home, plus a $7 bento box for the plane ride
- Head to Daniel K. Inouye International Airport for departure

Day 1: Arrival & Kihei Base Camp Setup
- Arrive midday at Kahului Airport, book flights 3 months in advance for <$350 round-trip from the West Coast
- Pick up a 4-door sedan rental ($80/day total, split 4 ways = $20/person/day, student discount from Hertz)

- Check into a budget Kihei Airbnb ($120/night total, split 4 ways = $30/person/night, walking distance to public beaches)
- Late afternoon: Swim at Kamaole Beach Park (free entry, less crowded than resort beaches)
- Dinner: $10 fish tacos from Geste Shrimp Truck (local-owned, donates 10% of profits to Lahaina recovery efforts)
- Evening: Free sunset watch and bonfire on Kamaole Beach, s’mores for dessert

Day 2: Road to Hana First Leg & Camping
- Wake up at 8:30am, pack camping gear (bring your own sleeping bags, rent a tent for $15 total for the trip from the Maui Hostel gear library)
- Start the Road to Hana, stop at the following spots: Twin Falls (free, swim in natural swimming holes), Garden of Eden Arboretum (student discount $8 entry, iconic coastal views), and Ke’anae Point (free, black rock shoreline for photos)
- Lunch: $6 banana bread and $4 coconut water from a family-run roadside stand in Hana
- Check into Waianapanapa State Park campsite ($15/night total for the group, reserve 3 months in advance) – set up camp near the famous black sand beach
- Evening: Cook hot dogs over the campfire, play card games, and stargaze (no cell service here, perfect for group bonding)

Day 3: Road to Hana Second Leg & Return to Kihei
- Wake up at 9am, hike Pipiwai Trail (4 mile round-trip, moderate, free entry with campsite reservation) – swim under 400-foot Waimoku Falls, walk through a 100-foot tall bamboo forest, and snap photos of the giant banyan tree (a viral TikTok spot)
- Stop at Ohe’o Gulch (Seven Sacred Pools, free entry) for a post-hike swim
- Drive back down the Road to Hana, stop for late lunch at Bruddah Hutt’s Food Truck in Pāʻia Town ($9 kalua pork plate, student discount)
- Arrive back at the Kihei Airbnb by 7pm, shower, and crash after two days of hiking and driving
- Late night snack: $5 lilikoi shave ice from Ululani’s Shave Ice near the Airbnb

Day 4: Upcountry Maui & Haleakala Sunset
- Wake up at 10am, no early alarms after the Road to Hana
- Drive up to Upcountry Maui, stop at Makawao Town (historic paniolo (cowboy) town, free to walk around) – browse thrift stores for vintage Hawaiian shirts ($5-$10 each) and grab $4 iced lattes from a student-run local coffee shop
- Stop at Ali’i Kula Lavender Farm (student discount $5 entry) to walk the lavender fields and get a $3 lavender lemonade
- Drive up to Haleakala National Park (vehicle entry $30, split 4 ways = $7.50/person, no reservation needed for entry after 3pm for sunset)
- Bring blankets, sweatshirts, and hot cocoa from the grocery run – temperatures hit 30-40°F at the summit! Watch the sunset over the volcanic crater
- Drive down after sunset, stop for late night $8 teriyaki plates at a Kahului food truck

Day 5: Molokini Snorkel & Karaoke Night
- Wake up at 9am, head to Maalaea Harbor for a group snorkel tour to Molokini Crater (student discount $40/person, includes gear, breakfast, and lunch, 10% of proceeds go to Lahaina recovery)
- Stop at Turtle Town on the way back from Molokini to swim with wild green sea turtles (free, no extra cost for the stop)
- Mid-afternoon: Lazy swim at Napili Bay (free entry, calm, clear waters)
- Evening: Walk the Kihei Farmers Market (free entry, open 4-8pm Thu-Sat) – get $3 fresh coconut, $5 mango sticky rice, and listen to local college students play live ukulele
- Late night: Karaoke at Kam Bowl in Kahului ($2 cover, $4 beer specials for students, private booths for groups)

Day 6: West Maui Hike & Community Luau
- Wake up at 8am, hike Waihe’e Ridge Trail (2.5 mile round-trip, moderate, free entry) – panoramic views of West Maui and the ocean, very few tourists here
- Stop at Kapalua Village Food Hall for lunch (all local vendors supporting Lahaina families) – $11 ahi poke bowl, student discount
- Mid-afternoon: Swim at D.T. Fleming Beach (free entry, great for beginner surfers, split a $5/hour board rental between 2 people)
- Evening: Attend the Maui United Way Community Luau in Wailuku ($30/person student rate, all proceeds go to Lahaina families) – includes all-you-can-eat local food, traditional hula, and fire knife performances
- Late night: Ice cream run to Dave’s Ice Cream in Wailuku ($5 scoops, try the lilikoi macadamia nut flavor)

Day 7: Last-Minute Adventures & Departure
- Sleep in until 10am, squeeze in a quick 1-hour group surf lesson at Kamaole Beach ($25 per person student rate)
- Stop at Leonard’s Malasadas kiosk in Kahului for $2 plain malasadas and a $4 haupia malasada to bring home
- Return the rental car, grab a $7 bento box from the airport food court for the plane ride
- Head to Kahului Airport for departure, stop at the local artist pop-up in the terminal to buy a $10 handmade print from a Maui high school student to support the community

- Check into Waianapanapa State Park campsite ($15/night total for the group, reserve 3 months in advance) – set up camp near the famous black sand beach
- Evening: Cook hot dogs over the campfire, play card games, stargaze (no cell service here, perfect for group bonding)

Day 3: Road to Hana Second Leg & Return to Kihei
- Wake up at 9am, hike Pipiwai Trail (4 mile round-trip, moderate, free entry with campsite reservation) – swim in Waimoku Falls, walk through the 100-foot tall bamboo forest, snap photos of the banyan tree (super viral on TikTok)
- Stop at Ohe'o Gulch (Seven Sacred Pools, free entry) for a post-hike swim
- Drive back down the Road to Hana, stop for late lunch at Bruddah Hutt's Food Truck in Pāʻia Town ($9 kalua pork plate, student discount)
- Arrive back at the Kihei Airbnb by 7pm, shower, crash after two days of hiking and driving
- Late night snack: $5 lilikoi shave ice from Ululani's Shave Ice near the Airbnb

Day 4: Upcountry Maui & Haleakala Sunset
- Wake up at 10am, no early alarms after the Road to Hana

- Stop at Ali'i Kula Lavender Farm (student discount $5 entry) to walk the lavender fields and get a $3 lavender lemonade
- Drive up to Haleakala National Park (vehicle entry $30, split 4 ways = $7.50/person, no reservation needed for entry after 3pm for sunset)
- Bring blankets, sweatshirts, and hot cocoa from the grocery run – it's 30-40 degrees at the summit! Watch the sunset over the crater, one of the most iconic views in Hawaii
- Drive down after sunset, stop for late night $8 teriyaki plates at a food truck in Kahului

Day 5: Molokini Snorkel & Karaoke Night

This rubric is designed to evaluate laptops for everyday consumer use, including remote work, student coursework, casual media consumption, and light to moderate gaming, with a 100-point total scale split evenly between performance metrics and price-to-value metrics, so neither category overshadows the other for users who need balanced function and affordability. The performance category, which totals 50 possible points, starts with an assessment of day-to-day responsiveness, which makes up 20 of those 50 performance points, because even a laptop with top-tier specs feels frustrating if it lags during routine tasks. Testers will measure boot time from a full shut down, with under 10 seconds earning full marks for that sub-measure, between 10 and 20 seconds earning half marks, and over 20 seconds earning no marks for that specific metric. Next, they will evaluate multitasking responsiveness by opening a common set of apps, including Google Chrome with 10 open tabs, a 50-page Microsoft Word document, a Zoom call running in the background, and a streaming service playing 1080p video, with no frame drops, input lag, or app crashes earning full marks for this portion of the responsiveness score. Minor lag only when switching between more than 8 active apps earns 75 percent of the possible marks for this sub-measure, consistent lag during routine multitasking earns 25 percent, and frequent crashes or inability to run three or more common apps at once earns no marks for this section. The next 15 points of the performance category are dedicated to specialized workload capacity, to account for users who occasionally need to run more demanding tools beyond basic browsing and document editing. This includes testing video export times for a 10-minute 1080p video in Adobe Premiere Pro, with export times under 2 minutes earning full marks for that sub-measure, between 2 and 5 minutes earning 75 percent, between 5 and 10 minutes earning half marks, and over 10 minutes earning a quarter of the available marks. Testers also assess light to moderate gaming performance as part of this section, running two popular mainstream titles, Fortnite and Stardew Valley, at medium settings and 1080p resolution, with consistent frame rates above 60 FPS for both titles earning full marks for that sub-measure. Frame rates between 30 and 60 FPS with no major stutters earn half marks, while frame rates below 30 FPS or frequent crashes during gameplay earn no marks for that section. For users who do photo editing, testers also measure load times for a 50-megapixel raw image in Adobe Lightroom, with load times under 2 seconds adding a small bonus of up to 1 point within the specialized workload section, to reward specs that benefit creative users without penalizing laptops built exclusively for basic use. The remaining 15 points of the performance category go to battery life and thermal performance, which are often overlooked but critical for real-world use outside of a home office setup. Battery life is tested with a standardized continuous use test, where the laptop is set to 50% brightness, connected to Wi-Fi, and streaming 1080p video while running a background email sync and a single open Word document, with 10 hours or more of continuous use earning full marks for that sub-measure. Battery life between 7 and 9 hours earns 75 percent, between 4 and 6 hours earns half marks, and under 4 hours earns no marks for battery life. Thermal performance is tested during a 30-minute sustained workload, exporting the same 10-minute video used in the specialized workload testing, with the laptop’s external chassis staying under 35 degrees Celsius at the palm rests and keyboard, and no audible fan noise that can be heard from 3 feet away earning full marks for thermal and noise performance. Chassis temperatures between 35 and 40 degrees or faint fan noise under heavy load earn 75 percent, temperatures over 40 degrees at the palm rests or loud fan noise that interferes with phone calls or media playback earn half marks, and thermal throttling that reduces processing speed by 20 percent or more during sustained use earns no marks for that section.

Moving to the price-to-value category, which makes up the other 50 total points, the first 20 points are allocated to baseline value alignment, which compares the laptop’s tested performance against market rates for comparable hardware. To calculate this, testers compile the average price of laptops with identical or nearly identical core specs, including processor generation, RAM capacity, storage type and size, and display resolution, across major retailers like Amazon, Best Buy, and the brand’s official website at the time of testing. If the laptop’s retail price is 15 percent or more below the average price for comparable spec laptops, it earns full marks for baseline value alignment, if it is between 5 percent below and 5 percent above the average, it earns 75 percent of the possible marks, if it is between 5 and 15 percent above the average, it earns half marks, and if it is 20 percent or more above the average for comparable specs, it earns no marks for that section. Within this baseline value section, there is a small adjustment for build quality, where a laptop with a durable aluminum chassis, spill-resistant keyboard, or military-grade durability certification can earn up to 2 extra points if it is priced at or below the average for comparable specs, as these features add long-term value that is not always reflected in raw spec sheets. The next 15 points of the price category go to included features and long-term cost of ownership, which account for perks that reduce the need for additional purchases or extend the laptop’s usable lifespan. First, testers evaluate included connectivity and accessories: if the laptop comes with a full-size HDMI port, two or more USB-A ports, a SD card reader, and a compatible charger in the box, without requiring users to purchase separate adapters for common peripherals like monitors, external hard drives, or cameras, it earns full marks for included connectivity features. If it requires one adapter for a common peripheral it earns 75 percent, if it requires two or more adapters for routine use it earns half marks, and if it does not include a charger in the box at all it earns no marks for that sub-measure. Long-term cost of ownership also includes assessing the ease of repair and upgradeability, with laptops that allow users to replace the RAM, storage, and battery at home with standard tools, without voiding the warranty, earning full marks for that sub-measure. Laptops that only allow storage upgrades earn half marks, and laptops that have all components soldered to the motherboard, making repairs or upgrades impossible without professional, costly service, earn no marks for that section. Warranty length factors in here as well, with a 3-year or longer manufacturer warranty that covers hardware defects and accidental damage adding up to 2 extra points within this section, while a 1-year warranty that only covers manufacturing defects is considered the baseline, and a warranty shorter than 1 year results in a 2-point deduction, as shorter warranties increase the risk of unexpected repair costs shortly after purchase. The remaining 15 points of the price category go to use-case specific value, which adjusts the score to reflect how well the laptop meets the needs of its target audience, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all standard. For example, a budget laptop priced under $500 intended for high school students who only need to write papers, browse the web, and attend virtual classes is not penalized for lacking a high-end graphics card or 4K display, as those features would add unnecessary cost for its target user, and instead earns marks based on how well it delivers on the core needs of its intended audience at its price point. To assess this, testers first identify the brand’s stated target audience for the laptop, whether that is budget students, remote professionals, content creators, or gaming enthusiasts, then compare its features and performance against the top priorities of that group, with a laptop that meets 90 percent or more of the core needs of its target audience at a price point 10 percent or below the average for that use case earning full marks for use-case specific value. If a laptop meets 70 to 89 percent of its target audience’s core needs and is priced within 10 percent of the average for that use case, it earns 75 percent of the possible marks, if it meets 50 to 69 percent of core needs or is priced 10 to 20 percent above the average for its use case, it earns half marks, and if it meets fewer than 50 percent of its target audience’s core needs or is priced 20 percent or more above the average for that use case, it earns no marks for that section. There is also a small penalty for misleading marketing claims within this section, for example, if a brand advertises a laptop as a “gaming device” but it cannot run even casual games at 30 FPS, or advertises “all-day battery life” but only delivers 3 hours of continuous use, that results in a 3-point deduction from the use-case value score, as deceptive marketing erodes the overall value of the product for consumers who purchase it based on those claims.

Once all performance and price points are tallied, the total score translates to a clear performance and value rating that consumers can use to make purchasing decisions. A total score of 90 to 100 indicates an exceptional laptop that offers class-leading performance at an outstanding price point, with no major flaws that would detract from everyday use, and is a top recommendation for almost any user in its target audience. A score of 80 to 89 indicates a very good laptop that offers strong performance and solid value, with only minor drawbacks like slightly loud fan noise under load or a single missing port that most users can work around easily. A score of 70 to 79 indicates a good laptop that meets most basic needs at a fair price, but may have noticeable tradeoffs like shorter battery life or limited upgradeability that users should consider before purchasing, especially if they plan to use the laptop for more than 2 or 3 years. # job title: front end & shelf stock associate, clifford blu
job type: hourly, part-time and full-time openings available
location: all metro clifford blu store locations

## job overview
clifford blu is a playful, community-focused lifestyle brand selling affordable apparel, home goods, and small gifts for people of all ages and interests. this dual role combines front end cashier duties with regular shelf stock monitoring to keep our stores running smoothly and our customers happy. you’ll be the first face most customers see when they check out, and a key part of making sure our most popular items never stay out of stock for long.

## core responsibilities
- operate the cash register accurately, processing all cash, credit, debit, gift card, and contactless transactions, plus returns, exchanges, and price adjustments
- greet every customer at the register with warmth, answer questions about current promotions, store policies, and product locations, and thank them for their visit after their transaction
- walk the full sales floor every 30 minutes (and as needed during slow periods) to check stock levels on all apparel, home, and accessory shelves
- log low or out-of-stock items in the shared store digital tracker, noting specific skus, sizes, and colors, and alert the floor lead immediately if a high-demand item is running low
- tidy folded items, straighten shelf displays, and restock small, easily accessible items (like keychains, stickers, and socks) during downtime between customers
- help bag purchases neatly, and alert customers to upcoming store events or loyalty program perks during checkout
- follow all store safety and loss prevention protocols, including checking for counterfeit bills and verifying id for age-restricted purchases

## required qualifications
- 1+ year of retail, cashier, or customer service experience preferred, but not required for motivated candidates eager to learn
- strong people skills to connect with a wide range of customers, resolve small concerns (like a missing product or return question) calmly, and collaborate with other store associates throughout shifts
- attention to detail to catch transaction errors at the register and spot low stock levels before items sell out entirely
- ability to stand for full 4-8 hour shifts, bend, reach, and lift up to 15 pounds to check stock on high and low shelves
- basic math skills to count cash and make change accurately, with training provided on our store point of sale system
- availability to work flexible hours, including weekends, holiday shifts, and occasional evening in-store events

## what we offer
- hourly pay starting at $15.50, with performance-based raises after a 90-day probationary period
- 25% off all clifford blu merchandise, including sale items and limited-edition drops, for you and one household member
- flexible scheduling for people balancing school, caregiving, other part-time roles, or personal commitments
- ongoing training to build your retail skills, customer service abilities, and inventory management knowledge, with clear paths to promotion to floor lead or store management roles for high performers
- access to exclusive store events, free product samples, and monthly team get-togethers outside of work hours
- paid time off for all full-time associates, plus eligibility for our store health insurance plan after 6 months of employment

clifford blu is an equal opportunity employer, and we encourage people of all backgrounds, identities, and experience levels to apply.

THE MILLER FAMILY’S ANNUAL FALL CAMPING TRIP KICKED OFF BEFORE DAWN ON A CRISP OCTOBER SATURDAY, THEIR DENTED NAVY MINIVAN PACKED TO THE ROOF WITH FLANNEL SLEEPING BAGS, A DENTED COOLER FULL OF HOT DOGS AND HOMEMADE MARSHMALLOWS, 11-YEAR-OLD MAEVE’S DOG-EARED FIELD GUIDE TO NORTH AMERICAN BIRDS, 8-YEAR-OLD OLLIE’S ENTIRE COLLECTION OF PLASTIC DINOSAURS, AND THEIR GRUMPY 10-YEAR-OLD BEAGLE, BISCUIT, WHO HAD STOLEN A PACK OF GRAPE FRUIT SNACKS OFF THE KITCHEN COUNTER BEFORE THEY EVEN LEFT THE DRIVEWAY.

DAD TOM DROVE THE WINDING BACKROADS TO WHITETAIL RIDGE STATE FOREST, SINGING OFF-KEY TO 90S COUNTRY, WHILE MOM EMMA TAPED CONSTRUCTION PAPER BANNERS THAT READ “CAMP MILLER 2024” TO THE BACK OF THE FRONT SEATS. WHEN THEY PULLED INTO THEIR RESERVED SITE—TUCKED BETWEEN TWO GIANT HEMLOCK TREES, A BABBLING CREEK LESS THAN A HUNDRED YARDS AWAY—OLLIE BOLTED OUT OF THE VAN BEFORE TOM EVEN PUT IT IN PARK, YELLING ABOUT PINE CONES THAT LOOKED EXACTLY LIKE T-REX TEETH.

SETTING UP THE TENT TOOK TWICE AS LONG AS ADVERTISED: TOM FORGOT THE INSTRUCTION MANUAL AT HOME, MAEVE LAUGHED SO HARD AT HIM FUMBLING WITH THE FIBERGLASS POLES THAT SHE SNORTED HOT APPLE CIDER OUT HER NOSE, AND BISCUIT DRAGGED A TENT STAKE INTO THE CREEK AND REFUSED TO RETRIEVE IT. BY THE TIME THEY HAD THE CANVAS STRUNG TIGHT AND THE CAMPFIRE LIT, THE SUN WAS DIPPING BELOW THE TREE LINE, PAINTING THE SKY SHADES OF FIERY ORANGE AND SOFT LAVENDER.

THEIR FIRST NIGHT WAS PERFECT IN THE WAY ONLY CAMP NIGHTS CAN BE: THEY ROASTED HOT DOGS UNTIL THE CASINGS CRACKED AND OOZED JUICE, MAEVE SPOTTED A BARRED OWL PERCHED ON A LOW BRANCH AND TICKED IT OFF HER BIRD GUIDE CHECKLIST, OLLIE BURNED THREE MARSHMALLOWS IN A ROW AND INSISTED THE CHARRED BLACK LUMPS WERE “PREHISTORIC S’MORES FOR HIS T-REXES,” AND EMMA TOLD GHOST STORIES SO SILLY THAT EVEN BISCUIT STOPPED NAPPING TO BARK AT THE PUNCHLINES.

ON SUNDAY MORNING, THEY SET OFF ON A TWO-MILE HIKE TO THE HIDDEN WATERFALL THE PARK RANGER HAD MENTIONED AT CHECK-IN. OLLIE TUCKED HIS FAVORITE STUFFED TRICERATOPS, SPIKE, INTO THE HOOD OF HIS FLEECE JACKET, PROMISING HE’D LET SPIKE “SEE THE WATERFALL FIRST BEFORE ANY HUMANS.” THEY HIKED PAST MUSHROOMS THAT LOOKED LIKE RED POLKA-DOT UMBRELLAS, CLIMBED OVER FALLEN LOGS COVERED IN BRIGHT NEON GREEN MOSS, AND STOPPED EVERY FEW FEET SO MAEVE COULD LISTEN FOR THE DISTINCT RAP OF PILEATED WOODPECKERS.

HALFWAY BACK TO CAMP, OLLIE FROZE MID-STEP, HIS FACE CRUMPLING LIKE A WAD OF WET TISSUE. “SPIKE’S GONE,” HE WHISPERED, BEFORE BURSTING INTO HEAVY, SHAKING SOBS. THEY BACKTRACKED THE ENTIRE TRAIL, CALLING SPIKE’S NAME, PEERING UNDER BUSHES AND BEHIND MOSSY ROCKS, BUT THE STUFFED TRICERATOPS WAS NOWHERE TO BE FOUND. BY THE TIME THEY TRUDGED BACK TO CAMP AS THE SUN SET, OLLIE’S EYES WERE RED AND SWOLLEN, AND HE REFUSED TO EAT EVEN HIS FAVORITE CHOCOLATE CHIP S’MORE.

THAT NIGHT, LONG AFTER MAEVE AND OLLIE HAD CRAWLED INTO THEIR SLEEPING BAGS, EMMA AND TOM WERE SITTING BY THE DYING FIRE, TALKING ABOUT STOPPING AT A TOY STORE ON THE WAY HOME TO BUY OLLIE A NEW STUFFED DINOSAUR, WHEN THEY HEARD A SOFT, DELIBERATE RUSTLE IN THE BUSHES AT THE EDGE OF THEIR SITE. TOM GRABBED THE HEAVY-DUTY FLASHLIGHT, SHINING IT TOWARD THE NOISE—AND THERE, STANDING RIGHT AT THE EDGE OF THE CAMP LIGHT, WAS A TINY JUVENILE FOX, ITS RED FUR FLUFFED THICK AGAINST THE COLD, SPIKE THE TRICERATOPS CLENCHED GENTLY IN ITS MOUTH BY THE SCUFFED HORN.

THE FOX TILTED ITS HEAD, DROPPED SPIKE ON THE DIRT AT THE EDGE OF THE FIRE RING, AND SAT BACK ON ITS HAUNCHES, LIKE IT WAS WAITING FOR A THANK YOU. EMMA GASPED, AND TOM CALLED OUT SOFTLY, “HEY, LITTLE GUY.” BEFORE THEY COULD MOVE TO GRAB A CRACKER OR A SMALL TREAT (THEY’D LATER AGREE IT WAS BETTER THEY DIDN’T FEED IT), THE FOX TURNED AND TROTTED BACK INTO THE DARK WOODS, ITS BUSHY WHITE-TIPPED TAIL DISAPPEARING BETWEEN THE HEMLOCK TRUNKS.

OLLIE WAS ASLEEP SO HARD THEY DIDN’T WAKE HIM UNTIL DAWN, WHEN THEY HANDED HIM HIS MUDDY, SLIGHTLY FOX-TOOTHED SPIKE. HIS FACE LIT UP SO BRIGHT IT OUTSHONE THE RISING SUN SIFTING THROUGH THE TREES. “THE FOREST FAIRIES BROUGHT HIM BACK!” HE YELLED, HUGGING SPIKE SO TIGHT HIS KNUCKLES TURNED WHITE.

ON THEIR WAY OUT OF THE CAMPGROUND MONDAY MORNING, OLLIE TAPED A CRAYON DRAWING OF SPIKE AND A RED FOX TO THE TRUNK OF THE BIG HEMLOCK BY THEIR SITE, WITH A NOTE SCRAWLED IN HIS MESSY, BUBBLY HANDWRITING: “THANK YOU FOR BRINGING SPIKE HOME. LOVE, OLLIE AND SPIKE.”

THE MILLERS DROVE AWAY WITH BISCUIT NAPPING ON OLLIE’S LAP, MAEVE FLIPPING THROUGH HER BIRD GUIDE TO HAND-WRITE “MAGIC FOREST FOX” INTO THE BLANK BACK PAGE OF UNDOCUMENTED SIGHTINGS, AND TOM AND EMMA GRINNING AT EACH OTHER IN THE FRONT SEAT, ALREADY COUNTING DOWN THE 362 DAYS UNTIL NEXT YEAR’S CAMPING TRIP.

**Startup Pitch: TrustClear**  
[Delivered to seed-stage investors, opening with a conversational, urgent tone]  

Last year, my 38-year-old sister Lila—an elementary school teacher, single mom to two 7-year-olds, owner of a $280k suburban home, and holder of a $120k 401(k) she barely thought about—laughed when I suggested she get a trust. “That’s for millionaires, right?” she said. Three months later, she was killed in a hit-and-run. Her kids spent 6 weeks in temporary state care while the court probated her handwritten will, and her estranged ex-husband gained control of her home equity to pay off $100k in gambling debts. That didn’t have to happen.

I’m Maeve Carter, founder of TrustClear, and we’re democratizing revocable living trusts—the single most powerful tool to protect families from probate, court interference, and asset loss—for the 70% of U.S. households that qualify but can’t access traditional estate planning. Let’s bust the biggest myth in personal finance: Trusts aren’t just for the 1%. They let you name permanent guardians for kids, set spending rules for heirs, skip probate (which costs an average of $14,000 and takes 6+ months for middle-class estates, per the American Bar Association), and even set aside funds for pets or aging parents. But 62% of U.S. adults have no estate plan at all, per Nolo, because traditional trusts cost $2,000–$5,000, require 3+ in-person attorney meetings, take 6 weeks to finalize, and worst of all: 60% of people who get trusts never fund them (meaning they’re legally useless) because attorneys leave that complicated administrative work to the client, per the 2023 Estate Planning Journal.

TrustClear solves every one of these pain points. Our AI-powered, attorney-vetted platform walks users through a 15-minute adaptive quiz that customizes to their unique situation: single parents, blended families, gig workers with business assets, pet owners, you name it. We instantly generate a state-specific trust document that’s reviewed by a licensed estate attorney in the user’s state within 48 hours, for a flat $299 fee—no hidden costs, no in-person meetings. Unlike competitors like LegalZoom, whose generic trust offering starts at $399, takes 2 weeks to process, and leaves funding entirely up to users, we include a personalized step-by-step funding checklist, and offer a $99 add-on to handle home and vehicle title transfers for you. We also send annual check-ins to update your trust for free when you have a kid, buy a home, get married, or divorce, plus a secure digital vault to share documents with trustees and beneficiaries.

In 8 months of beta testing across 12 U.S. states, we’ve served 2,100+ customers, earned a 4.9/5 Trustpilot rating, and partnered with 14 credit unions and employer benefits platforms to offer TrustClear as a core employee benefit—those partnerships drove 40% of our new sign-ups last quarter. The U.S. estate planning market is $22B annually, growing 7% a year, and 78 million Millennials and 65 million Gen Zers are entering peak asset-accumulation years, with 80% saying they prefer digital, on-demand financial services over traditional law firms, per eMarketer.

We’re raising $1.2M in seed funding to expand to all 50 states by Q1 2025, launch our small business trust offering for freelancers and gig workers, and scale our benefits partner program. Our projections show we’ll hit 20,000 customers and $7M in ARR by the end of 2025, with a 72% gross margin, thanks to our AI that cuts attorney review time by 70%.

Lila’s story isn’t an anomaly: 1,700 Americans die every day without an estate plan, leaving their families to navigate costly, traumatic court battles. TrustClear isn’t just selling legal documents—we’re selling peace of mind that’s accessible to every person who’s worked hard to build something they want to protect. We’re turning a luxury for the wealthy into a basic financial safety net for everyone. Thank you. (Word count: 987)

first names are the first gift we receive that we don’t ask for, stitched to our birth certificates before we can blink, before we have preferences or quirks or a favorite flavor of ice cream. they stick to us like second skin, even when they don’t fit at first, even when we hate the way adults drawl the full three syllables when we’re in trouble, even when we shorten them or swap them for a middle name or a nickname made of half a word and an inside joke. some names carry the weight of generations, passed down from grandfathers and aunts and distant cousins we never met, so that every time someone says it, they’re also saying the name of the farmer who homesteaded a hundred acres in 1920, the teacher who taught three generations of kids to read, the teenager who snuck out to go to jazz shows in the 1970s. other names are new, cobbled together from song lyrics and nature walks and favorite characters from books, so that they carry the echo of a parent’s favorite song, the way the sun hit a lake the day they found out they were expecting, the comfort of a story that got them through a hard year. we rename ourselves too, when the name we were given doesn’t fit the person we grow into, picking a sound that sits soft in our mouths, that feels like home when we say it out loud, that lets the world see the version of ourselves we’ve always known we are.


jasper was the name my mother almost gave me, before she settled on the softer, plainer one i’ve carried my whole life. i used to test it out when i was a kid, whispering it under my breath when i walked the woods behind our house, when i climbed the old oak tree at the edge of the yard, when i pretended i was a brave explorer instead of a shy kid who was scared to talk to cashiers. that name felt like a parallel life, the version of me that wasn’t afraid to raise their hand in class, that didn’t cry when they fell off their bike, that talked to new kids like they were already friends. every name carries these little ghosts, the people who wore it before us, the people we associate it with, the characters from books and shows that tuck themselves into the edges of the sound. a name can make you think of the friend who taught you to skip stones, the barista who always remembers your order, the stranger you saw laughing in a park once who felt familiar even though you never spoke. when you meet someone who shares your first name, it’s like holding up a mirror to a part of yourself you didn’t know existed, like finding a distant cousin who carries the same small, invisible mark as you, even if you have nothing else in common.


there is a quiet magic in saying someone’s first name right, in rolling the syllables off your tongue the way they like them, no shortening, no misspelling, no assumption. it’s the smallest act of recognition, a way to say i see you, i remember you, you are not just a face in a crowd. when someone is sad, saying their first name soft, like you’re holding something fragile, can be more comforting than any long speech, any hug, any gift you could buy. when you’re excited, yelling someone’s first name across a crowded room is a signal, a beacon, cutting through all the noise to say i’m here, i found you, i’m so glad you exist. even the names we don’t say out loud anymore carry weight, the names of people who have left, who moved across the world, who died, who we don’t talk to anymore. tucking those names into the back of your throat, letting them sit soft there, is a way to carry the people we loved with us, even when they’re not around. first names are just sounds, at the end of the day, vibrations in the air that we’ve agreed mean something, that we’ve agreed to carry for each other, small and warm and ours, for as long as we want them.

I froze when I was jogging my usual tree-lined suburban trail last Saturday, the kind of crisp fall evening where the air smells like wood smoke and crushed apple cider donuts from the farm stand at the trailhead. I’d been pushing for a new personal best, my breath coming in steady puffs and my workout playlist thumping in my earbuds, when a sharp, echoing CRUNCH from the thick underbrush 15 feet to my left ripped me right out of my rhythm.

I’d brushed off my best friend’s warning to carry protection on solo dusk jogs for months, but in that split second, I was suddenly grateful I’d stuffed a mini can of PEPPER SPRAY into the pocket of my running vest that morning on a whim. I ripped out my earbuds, my heart hammering so hard I could feel it in my fingertips, and squinted into the long, stretching shadows—until two glowing, amber eyes blinked back at me. For a split, panicky second, I thought it was a coyote, or even a lost black bear, like the ones the local parks department had been issuing alerts about all month. But then a massive 12-point buck stepped into the slanted orange glow of the setting sun, its antlers so wide they almost brushed the oak branches on either side of it.

I’d seen dozens of deer on this trail over the years, but never one this big, never one that didn’t bolt the second it caught a whiff of human sweat or cherry energy gel. I’d read a hiking blog the week prior that rutting season made male deer unpredictable, even aggressive, so I locked my knees and held perfectly still, not even daring to swallow too loud for fear of spooking him. For 10 whole seconds that felt like an hour, we stared each other down—until a plump, ripe ACORN dropped from the oak above his head and smacked him right between the ears. He flinched so hard he stumbled back a step, then tossed his head and bounded off into the underbrush, hooves thundering so loud they shook the carpet of fallen maple leaves at my feet.

I didn’t move for another 30 seconds, my lungs burning and my legs wobbly, until I remembered I’d stashed a pack of TRAIL MIX loaded with mini peanut butter cups in my vest as a post-jog reward, and the urge to dig it out to steady my nerves finally pushed me to unfreeze. I fumbled for my dimming HEADLAMP to light the last mile of the unlit trail, glancing up to see the bright, round FULL MOON peeking through the treetops, its silver glow turning the pine needles pale and ghostly. When I finally stumbled into the trailhead parking lot, I almost walked straight into a bright yellow sign the parks department had hammered into a post that morning that blared CAUTION: ACTIVE WILDLIFE — a warning I’d breezed right past an hour earlier, too focused on beating my personal best to glance up.

I laughed shakily as I unlocked my car, popping a peanut butter cup into my mouth and making a mental note to never again zone out so hard on a solo jog, and to always, always check the trail alerts before I laced up my sneakers. That split second of freezing wasn’t just fear—it was the sharp, sudden reminder that even the most familiar, boring local trail could hold a surprise big enough to stop me mid-stride.

# The Fractured Umma: Unpacking the Historical, Theological, and Communal Differences Between Sunni and Shi’a Muslims
In the aftermath of the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq, global media outlets began framing the country’s rising violence as an ancient, inevitable conflict between two warring sects of Islam: Sunni and Shi’a. Headlines portrayed the two groups as eternal enemies, bound by 1,400 years of religious hatred, with little attention paid to their shared core beliefs or the political forces driving modern sectarian tension. This narrative is both oversimplified and dangerous. As the world’s second-largest religion, with 1.9 billion adherents spanning every continent, Islam’s two major branches—85% Sunni and 15% Shi’a—are united by a commitment to the Quran, the prophecy of Muhammad, and the core tenets of the faith, but diverge sharply over questions of religious authority, communal identity, and historical memory. What began as a narrow political dispute over succession to the Prophet in 632 CE evolved over 14 centuries into distinct theological, ritual, and communal identities, shaped by centuries of persecution, imperial power struggles, and colonial manipulation. To understand these differences is to reject the myth of inherent sectarian violence and recognize that the umma (global Muslim community)’s fractures are as much political as they are religious.

The origins of the Sunni-Shi’a split lie not in theological disagreement, but in a crisis of political legitimacy following the Prophet Muhammad’s unexpected death in Medina in 632 CE. Muhammad, who had served as both spiritual leader and political ruler of the growing Muslim community, left no clear heir, and no formal system for selecting a successor. As his family prepared his body for burial, a group of leading Muslim companions gathered at the Saqifah, a meeting hall in Medina, to choose a new leader (caliph, or “successor”). The majority of companions backed Abu Bakr, Muhammad’s closest friend, father-in-law, and one of the earliest converts to Islam, arguing that leadership of the community should be decided by consensus (ijma) of the most pious and qualified members. Abu Bakr was elected the first of the “Rightly Guided Caliphs” (Rashidun), a line that would include Umar ibn al-Khattab, Uthman ibn Affan, and finally Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law.

But a smaller faction, soon known as the Shi’at Ali (the Partisans of Ali), rejected the Saqifah election as illegitimate. They argued that Muhammad had explicitly designated Ali as his successor during a sermon at Ghadir Khumm, a site on the road between Mecca and Medina, where he had declared, “He whose mawla (master, patron, or friend) I am, Ali is his mawla.” For Shi’a, this statement was a formal divine appointment: Ali, as a member of the Ahl al-Bayt (the Prophet’s immediate family), was the only rightful heir to both spiritual and political authority. Ali was passed over for the caliphate three times, only assuming power in 656 CE after the assassination of Uthman. His reign was marred by the first Muslim civil war (fitna), as Mu’awiya, the governor of Syria, challenged Ali’s legitimacy in the wake of Uthman’s death. Ali was assassinated by a dissident in 661 CE, and Mu’awiya founded the Umayyad Caliphate, a dynastic empire that would rule most of the Muslim world for the next century.

The defining event that cemented Shi’a identity as a distinct community came in 680 CE, when Ali’s younger son Husayn led a small band of 72 followers, including women and children, to challenge the tyrannical rule of the Umayyad caliph Yazid. Outnumbered by thousands of Umayyad soldiers in the desert of Karbala, in modern-day Iraq, Husayn and his entire retinue were massacred, their bodies mutilated and their families taken prisoner in Damascus. For Shi’a, Karbala is not merely a historical event: it is the foundational myth of their communal identity, a symbol of the struggle of the oppressed against corrupt, illegitimate power, and a testament to the willingness of the Ahl al-Bayt to sacrifice everything for the truth of Islam. As the popular Shi’a maxim puts it, “Every day is Ashura, every land is Karbala,” framing the fight against injustice as a perpetual, sacred duty. For Sunni Muslims, by contrast, the Rashidun caliphs are all viewed as legitimate, pious rulers, and Karbala is remembered as a tragic civil war, not a defining moral parable of persecution. This difference in historical memory would lay the groundwork for the theological divergences that emerged in the centuries after the split.

Over the first three centuries of Islamic history, what began as a political dispute evolved into starkly different theological frameworks, centered above all on the question of religious authority. For Sunni Muslims, authority is derived from four sources: the Quran (the literal word of God), the Sunnah (the Prophet’s sayings and actions, preserved in vetted hadith collections compiled by scholars such as al-Bukhari and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj), ijma (consensus of the community of scholars), and qiyas (analogical reasoning). Sunni leadership is deliberately decentralized: there is no single, central religious authority, and scholars (ulama) are valued for their expertise in Islamic law (sharia) but are not considered infallible. Political leaders, from caliphs to modern heads of state, are tasked with enforcing sharia but have no special spiritual status; the only human who was infallible, for Sunni, was Muhammad himself.

For Shi’a Muslims, by contrast, the central theological doctrine is the Imamate: the belief that God appointed a line of 12 infallible, sinless Imams (for the largest Shi’a subgroup, the Twelvers) from the bloodline of Muhammad, beginning with Ali. These Imams are not merely political rulers: they are divinely guided interpreters of the Quran and sharia, endowed with esoteric knowledge of the faith that no ordinary human can access. Twelver Shi’a believe that the 12th Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into occultation (ghayba) in 874 CE, hidden by God until the end of time, when he will return as the messianic Mahdi to restore justice and defeat evil on earth. In the absence of the Hidden Imam, religious authority falls to marjas al-taqlid (sources of emulation), senior scholars whose rulings on religious law are binding on the Shi’a who choose to follow them. This system of a centralized, living religious authority is unique to Shi’a Islam, and stands in sharp contrast to Sunni Islam’s decentralized scholarly tradition. Shi’a also differ from Sunni in their approach to the Quran, prioritizing ta’wil (allegorical, esoteric interpretation) to uncover the hidden meanings of the text, rather than the literal interpretation favored by most Sunni schools of jurisprudence. Shi’a also practice intercession, believing that the Imams and saints can intercede with God on behalf of believers—a practice that conservative Sunni groups such as the Wahhabis of Saudi Arabia reject as shirk (polytheism), a grave sin against the oneness of God.

These theological differences are embodied in distinct ritual practices that mark Sunni and Shi’a identity, even as both groups adhere to the five core pillars of Islam. The shahada (profession of faith), the first pillar, is almost identical: Sunni recite, “There is no god but God, Muhammad is the messenger of God,” while Shi’a add the phrase “and Ali is the wali (friend and patron) of God” to affirm their belief in Ali’s divine appointment. For salat (daily prayer), Sunni Muslims pray five times a day, standing with their hands folded over their chests, and prostrate on any clean surface, usually a woven prayer rug. Most Shi’a combine the five daily prayers into three sessions (merging midday and afternoon, sunset and night prayers, as permitted by their jurisprudence), pray with their hands at their sides, and prostrate on a small clay disk called a turbah, usually made from soil from Karbala, to replicate the Prophet’s practice of praying on natural earth, rather than man-made materials. Shi’a also practice an additional religious tax, khums, a 20% levy on annual surplus income, half of which is given to the poor and half to marjas to fund religious schools, shrines, and charitable work; Sunni only pay the mandatory zakat, a 2.5% tax on accumulated wealth.

The most visible ritual difference, however, is the commemoration of Ashura, the 10th day of the Islamic month of Muharram, which marks the anniversary of Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala. For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a voluntary day of fasting, commemorating God’s deliverance of the Israelites from Pharaoh. For Shi’a, it is the holiest day of mourning in the religious calendar, marked by weeks of majalis (mourning gatherings) where scholars recite the story of Karbala, and marsiyas (elegies) for Husayn are sung. In many Shi’a communities, processions are held where mourners beat their chests or whip themselves to share in Husayn’s suffering, though most modern Shi’a marjas have condemned self-flagellation, encouraging mourners to donate blood or give to charity instead. Shi’a also place great importance on ziyara (pious visits) to the shrines of the Imams, including the tombs of Ali in Najaf, Husayn in Karbala, and the 8th Imam Reza in Mashhad, Iran—sites that draw millions of pilgrims every year, and are considered nearly as sacred as Mecca for many Shi’a. Sunni Muslims also venerate the Prophet’s family, but conservative Sunni movements reject shrine pilgrimage as bid’ah (heretical innovation), viewing it as a form of idolatry.

Over the centuries, these theological and ritual differences were shaped by shifting power dynamics that deepened communal identity, and in the modern era, have been exploited for political gain. For most of Islamic history, Shi’a were a persecuted minority: the Umayyad, Abbasid, and Ottoman caliphates were all Sunni-led, and Shi’a communities faced discrimination, violence, and periodic campaigns of repression for rejecting the legitimacy of caliphal rule. This persecution cemented Shi’a identity as a community of resistance, bound by shared suffering and loyalty to the Ahl al-Bayt. The dynamic shifted dramatically in the 16th century, when the Safavid Empire made Twelver Shi’ism the state religion of Iran, forcibly converting the country’s majority Sunni population and establishing the first major Shi’a imperial power, setting off centuries of rivalry with the Sunni Ottoman Empire.

Modern sectarian tension, however, is largely a product of colonialism and post-colonial authoritarian rule. After the fall of the Ottoman Empire in World War I, British and French colonial powers drew arbitrary borders across the Middle East, creating nation-states where minority groups were often placed in power to divide opposition and maintain control: the French favored the Alawite minority (an offshoot of Shi’ism) in Syria, while the British installed a Sunni monarchy over the Shi’a majority in Iraq. The 1979 Iranian Revolution, which established the world’s first modern Shi’a theocracy, amplified these tensions: Saudi Arabia, the leading Sunni power in the region, responded by promoting its conservative Wahhabi ideology, which labels Shi’a as heretics, to counter Iranian influence across the Middle East. Authoritarian regimes in Iraq, Syria, and Bahrain have repeatedly exploited sectarian divisions to suppress opposition, framing dissent as a threat to communal stability. The result has been a wave of sectarian violence in the 21st century, from Iraq to Yemen, that is often misrepresented as a product of ancient religious hatred, rather than a deliberate political strategy.

Crucially, however, these differences and tensions obscure the far deeper common ground that unites Sunni and Shi’a Muslims. Both groups share a commitment to the oneness of God, the prophecy of Muhammad, the sanctity of the Quran, and the coming Day of Judgment. Both celebrate the same major holidays, including Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, and both have produced rich intellectual traditions that shaped global philosophy, science, and literature: Sunni scholars such as al-Ghazali, Ibn Sina, and Ibn Khaldun laid the groundwork for modern Islamic thought, while Shi’a thinkers such as Mulla Sadra and Allameh Tabatabai developed groundbreaking systems of philosophy and theology. In 2004, the Amman Message, issued by King Abdullah II of Jordan and endorsed by over 200 leading Sunni and Shi’a scholars from 50 countries, formally recognized both branches as legitimate expressions of Islam, forbade the practice of takfir (declaring another Muslim an apostate), and called for unity across the umma. For the vast majority of Muslims, in countries from Indonesia to Senegal to the United States, sectarian differences are a matter of personal piety, not conflict, and many reject sectarian labels entirely, identifying first and foremost as Muslim.

In the end, the split between Sunni and Shi’a Islam is a testament to the diversity of the Muslim community, and to the way that political disputes can evolve into deeply held religious identities over centuries. What began as a debate over who should lead the umma after Muhammad’s death grew into distinct traditions of theology, ritual, and historical memory, shaped by persecution, power, and culture. To reduce these differences to a story of ancient hatred is to erase the shared faith that unites 1.9 billion people, and to ignore the political forces that have manipulated sectarian identity for gain. Understanding the differences between Sunni and Shi’a is not just a matter of religious literacy: it is a necessary step toward building a more just and peaceful world, where the umma’s diversity is celebrated as a strength, not a source of division.

Japan’s recorded and prehistoric history spans over 40,000 years, shaped by alternating periods of isolation and cross-cultural exchange, centralized and feudal rule, and dramatic 19th–20th century transformation. The earliest distinct cultural era is the *Jōmon* period (c. 14,500–300 BCE), named for the cord-marked pottery produced by its semi-sedentary hunter-gatherer communities, among the oldest known ceramic traditions in the world. The subsequent Yayoi period (c. 300 BCE–300 CE) brought wet rice agriculture, iron and bronze technology, and social stratification from the East Asian mainland, laying the groundwork for the centralized Yamato state that emerged in the Kofun period (c. 300–538 CE) and established the unbroken imperial line that still formally rules Japan today.

In the 6th century CE, *Buddhism* was introduced to Japan from the Korean kingdom of Baekje, sparking widespread adoption of Chinese writing, legal systems, and imperial bureaucracy that defined the Asuka and Nara periods. The 794 CE move of the imperial capital to Heian-kyō (modern Kyoto) launched the Heian period, a golden age of indigenous aristocratic culture that produced *The Tale of Genji*, the world’s first full-length novel, as Chinese cultural influence waned. Hey Kai,
I heard from your guidance teacher at Aberdeen Grammar that you’ve been looking for low-effort, flexible ways to pad your UCAS application while doing something that actually matters for the city you grew up in—so I wanted to loop you in on a volunteer gig at Torry Soup Kitchen that’s made for teens like you.
Before you hit delete because you think volunteering means boring, stuffy work with people who have nothing in common with you, hear me out: this is nothing like the forced S3 charity days where you picked up litter at the Beach Esplanade and complained the whole time.
First, let’s talk perks, because I know you’re not going to sign up for something that doesn’t fit your chaotic teen schedule:
✅ A MASSIVE UCAS BOOST that admissions teams go crazy for. We write hyper-specific, glowing references for every regular volunteer that highlight exactly what you did (not generic garbage like “they’re a hard worker”) and 90% of our teen volunteers from last year said their reference from us was the thing that made their uni application stand out.
✅ FREE stovies, homemade lentil soup, and the best tablet in Aberdeenshire every single shift. We also stock Irn-Bru and chocolate digestives for volunteers, and the local Greggs drops off leftover doughnuts every Saturday—you’ll leave stuffed, no sad packed lunch required. We even cover your bus fare to and from the kitchen, so you don’t have to blow your pocket money on the 19 bus ride over.
✅ Bring a mate, no questions asked. We don’t stick you with a random group of boomers you have nothing in common with. Grab your best pal who’s also complaining there’s nothing to do on weekends, sign up for the same shift, and you can banter while you wipe down tables or hand out hot drinks to folks coming in.
✅ Total flexibility. I know you’ve got a part-time shift at the Vue, S5 prelims coming up, and tickets to that gig at The Tunnels next month. You can sign up for one shift a week, one shift a month, or even just a one-off to test it out. NO EXPERIENCE NEEDED, we’ll walk you through everything on your first day, and no one will yell at you if you spill a cup of tea.
Now, the part that matters: this work is CRUCIAL for our Aberdeen COMMUNITY. Last month, a 17-year-old from Bridge of Don started volunteering with us, and she told me she was terrified no one would talk to her on her first shift. Now, she spends every Saturday listening to old Ronnie, a former North Sea fisherman who’s been coming in for 3 years, tell wild stories about hauling cod in 20-foot waves, and she sneaks him extra tablet every week because it’s his favorite. She said it’s the most fun she has all week, way better than scrolling TikTok for 4 hours straight while waiting for the haar to lift.
This isn’t just about “giving back,” either. It’s about getting to know the city you call home in a way you never have before, hearing stories you’ll tell your own kids one day, and making a real, tangible difference for people who live 10 minutes from your house. The impact you’ll have is LIFE-CHANGING for the folks we serve, and it’s pretty great for you too.
Sign up takes 2 minutes—just click this link [link] to pick a shift that works for you, or shoot me a text at 07xxxxxxxxx if you have questions. Even if you only come for one shift, you’ll leave knowing you made someone’s day a little brighter.
See you in the toasty warm kitchen (no haar allowed),
Mia Robertson
Volunteer Coordinator
Torry Soup Kitchen

<<Mitä tapahtuu, kun haistat kukkaa?>>

Kun alat haistaa kukkaa, painat ensin nenäsi lähelle kukkaa ja hengität hitaasti, rauhallisesti sisään. Tiedätkö mitä salaisuutta tapahtuu seuraavaksi – vaikka et sitä millään näe?

Kukat lähettävät ympärilleen erittäin pieniä, täysin näkymättömiä hajuhiukkasia. Ne ovat niin kevyitä, että ne leijuvat rauhallisesti ilmassa ympäri kukkaa. Kun hengität sisään, nuo hiukkaset tulevat ilman mukana suoraan sisään nenääsi.

Nenän sisällä yläosassa on pieni, salainen alue, jossa on tuhansia erikoisia hajusoluja. Ne ovat kuin pienet hajuvartijat, jotka tarkkailevat kaikkea mitä tulee nenään sisään. Hajuhiukkaset tarttuvat näihin soluihin heti, ja seuraavana hetkenä hajusolut lähettävät supernopean viestin aivoillesi – kuin lähettäisit kaverillesi pikaviestein puhelimella, mutta vielä paljon nopeammin!

Aivosi saavat viestin heti, ja ne tunnistavat saman tien minkä kukan tuoksu on kyseessä. Jos haisit tuoksuvaa ruusua, aivot sanovat sinulle: "Oi, tämä on ihana ruusu!" Jos taas haistat makeaa kukkakkoa tai valmikasta lummelimea, ne tunnistavat hajun välittömästi. Siksi saatkin usein lämpimän, hyvän olon, kun haistat kaunista, tuoksuvaa kukkaa puistossa tai kodissa!

- Presented by: Jane Doe, CEO & Co-Founder

---

## Slide 2: The Problem
### Key Content:
The global board game community is fragmented, underserved, and locked into clunky, general-purpose tools:
1. **Fragmented Discovery & Connection**: Players bounce between BoardGameGeek (database-only, 20-year-old UI), Facebook Groups, Discord, and Reddit with no unified space for social connection, local meetups, and hobby tracking.
2. **Painful Playgroup Matching**: New, 68% of casual board game players report struggling to find local playgroups that match their skill level, schedule, and play style (source: 2024 BoardGameGeek Community Survey)
3. **No End-to-End Game Night Tooling**: Players use 5+ separate tools (Google Calendar, SignUpGenius, GroupMe, physical score pads, rule books for game nights, with zero integration.
4. **No Accessibility-First Matching**: Neurodivergent, disabled, and new players have no dedicated way to find playgroups that accommodate sensory needs, wheelchair access, or rule explanation support.
5. **Underserved Stakeholders**: Local game stores (FLGS), publishers, and board game creators lack a dedicated space to connect directly with their target audience, sell event tickets, and promote releases.
### Speaker Notes:
"Right now, if you want to play a physical board game with people you actually enjoy playing with, you have to jump through 7 different hoops. And if you’re a local game store or creator, there’s no way to reach your exact audience without fighting general social media algorithms that prioritize viral content over niche hobby needs.

---

## Slide 3: Our Solution
### Key Content:
MeepleMeet is the first mobile-first, end-to-end social network built exclusively for the global board game community, serving every part of the hobby journey:
- Hyper-personalized playgroup matching for in-person and remote play, with accessibility and play style compatibility scoring
- Integrated game night hub with digital scorekeeping, rule reference, RSVP tracking, and post-game recaps
- Dedicated profiles and monetization tools for FLGS, publishers, and board game content creators
- Built-in collection tracking, personalized game recommendations, and niche hobby groups
### Speaker Notes:
"We built MeepleMeet to be the one-stop shop for every board game moment. Whether you’re a new player looking for your first casual Catan night, a competitive tournament player looking for a tournament, a local game store promoting your next open play, or a creator sharing your latest miniature paint job, MeepleMeet is built for you.

---

Covers players, publishers, FLGS, content creators, and event organizers
#### SAM: 150M Global Monthly Active Board Game Players
40M+ dedicated hobbyists, 110M casual players who play 1+ times per month
#### SOM: 2M Active Users | $36M Annual Revenue by Year 3
### Speaker Notes:
"This isn’t a tiny niche hobby. Board games grew 20% during the pandemic, and growth has stayed steady as players crave in-person, low-screen social connection. We’re targeting a massive, fast-growing market that has never had a dedicated social network built for it.

---

1. **For Players**:

Diversified, low-intrusive revenue streams, no reliance on intrusive ads:

thread: the day i learned the earth isn’t flat didn’t happen in science class or on a bleary 2 a.m. youtube deep dive.
it happened behind a dilapidated rest stop off i-40 in west texas, next to a dumpster that reeked of pickled eggs and expired gas station hot dogs.
i was hiding from a crew of roving birthday clowns who’d tried to trade me a squeaky rubber chicken for my last bag of flamin’ hot cheetos.
a guy in a mold-stained raincoat caked with pecan shell dust leaned against the dumpster next to me, chewing something that crunched way too loud.
he didn’t even glance my way when he said you know the flat earth thing’s bullshit, right? like he was commenting on the dusty wind.
i blinked, because i’d spent the last three months deep in flat earth tiktok just to annoy my cousin who works a desk job at nasa.
i mumbled yeah, duh, obviously, even though i’d spent the week prior arguing that gravity was just a network of giant magnets buried under the dirt.
he spit a pecan shell into the dumpster and held out a crumpled map that looked like it had been chewed by a very determined raccoon.
the map wasn’t the flat disc with the ice wall i’d seen a hundred times online, it was all lumpy, like a squashed orange someone had sat on through a road trip.
he said he’d spent the last twelve years driving every potholed back road in the continental u.s. selling home-roasted pecans out of his beat-up minivan.
he said if the earth was flat, he’d have driven off the edge somewhere near el paso back in ‘18, when his gps died and he drove straight for three whole days.
i squinted, because that didn’t line up with the lore everyone shared online, right? the ice wall was guarded by penguins with tiny tasers, everyone knew that.
he laughed so hard he snort-laughed, and a half-chewed pecan chunk flew out of his nose and landed right on the toe of my scuffed white sneaker.
he pulled out a crinkled polaroid of him standing on a rocky beach in chile, next to a penguin that was definitely not holding a taser, just a very tiny silver fish.
he said he’d sailed across the atlantic the year prior to sell pecans to a convent of nuns in portugal who were obsessed with his salted roast.
he never hit an ice wall on that trip, he said, just a flock of very aggressive seagulls that stole half his snack supply mid-voyage.
i thought about all the nights i’d stayed up arguing with strangers online that lunar eclipses were just a giant shadow cat crossing the face of the sun.
i thought about how my nasa cousin had sent me a printed photo of the earth from the international space station for my birthday, and i’d mailed it back to her with “photoshop” scrawled across it in crayon.
i thought about the time i tried to dig a hole to the “bottom of the flat disc” in my backyard and only hit a sprinkler pipe that flooded my entire patio.
the pecan guy handed me a handful of warm, salted pecans and said people love believing weird shit because it makes the world feel smaller, easier to hold.
i nodded, because that quiet, offhand line hit way harder than any textbook or snarky debunk video ever had.
the clowns from earlier yelled my name from the rest stop parking lot, waving the rubber chicken over their heads like a battle flag.
the pecan guy winked, climbed into his van that had “pecan pete’s world famous nuts” painted on the side in chipped neon pink, and drove off.
i never saw him again, but i still have that crumpled lumpy map tucked in the glove box of my car, right next to my expired registration.
i texted my cousin that night and told her she was right about the earth not being flat, and she sent back twelve clown emojis and a link to a nasa merch store.
i still don’t fully trust big gravity, though, just in case the giant magnet thing is partially true.
and i still side-eye any penguin i see at the zoo, just in case the tiny taser lore was less of a lie than the flat disc was.

### Section 1
Elias Voss had worked the front desk of the Hawthorne District Public Library’s rare book room for three years before he met Maren Hale, and in that time, he’d developed a rigid, unchanging routine that he’d once bragged to his sister could survive a Category 5 hurricane or a surprise visit from their overly critical grandmother. He brewed chamomile tea at exactly 9:02 a.m. every weekday, timed so the steam stopped curling right as the first regulars wandered in. He arranged the brass library bookmarks by weight every morning, from the tiny, delicate leaf-shaped ones to the heavy vintage ones engraved with the library’s 1905 founding date. He wiped down the oak reading table with lemon oil every afternoon at 3:15, following the grain so carefully he could trace every scratch and water ring from memory. He even counted the 17 steps from the break room to the front desk every shift, noting the crack in the linoleum at step 12 that the city had been promising to fix for six months. His routine was his comfort, a set of small, predictable joys that kept the chaos of the world at bay, until Maren walked through the door on a rainy Tuesday in April. She was wearing faded canvas overalls stiff with milkweed sap, mud caked on the toes of her work boots, and a silver hoop earring shaped like a bumblebee dangling from her left ear. A tattoo of a monarch butterfly curled up her right forearm, peeking out from the sleeve of her flannel shirt, and she was clutching a crumpled list of book titles in one hand. She apologized profusely for tracking mud into the rare book room, gesturing at her boots with a sheepish grin, and Elias waved her off, telling her the library had seen far worse messes, including the time a retiree spilled a full bottle of maple syrup on a first edition of *Where the Wild Things Are* during a storytime event. She laughed, a bright, loud sound that echoed off the high, book-lined walls, and asked if he had a copy of the 1912 edition of *Pacific Northwest Wildflower and Pollinator Field Manual*, explaining that she ran a volunteer project restoring native pollinator corridors in the vacant lots along Burnside Street. Mid-sentence, she blinked hard, jerked her left shoulder up to her ear, and barked “HONEYCOMB!” so loud it made the brass bookmarks rattle on the desk. Elias didn’t flinch. He didn’t stare, or apologize, or ask if she was okay, or do any of the things most people did when they saw a tic for the first time. He just nodded, said “One sec, I know right where that is,” and turned to pull the leather-bound volume from the locked shelf behind him. Elias’s 12-year-old cousin Leo had been diagnosed with Tourette Syndrome when he was seven, so Elias had spent years learning not to react to tics, to treat them like any other harmless quirk, like Leo’s habit of chewing on the end of his hoodie string or his obsession with Minecraft. When Elias turned back with the book, Maren was staring at him, wide-eyed, like she’d just seen a ghost. “You didn’t… say anything,” she said, tilting her head, like she was trying to figure out if he was being polite or if he just hadn’t noticed. “About the tic, I mean.” Elias shrugged, setting the book on the table and pushing it toward her. “My cousin has Tourette’s. I’m used to random outbursts. Last week he yelled ‘CREEPER!’ mid-dinner and spilled his whole glass of lemonade on my mom’s new tablecloth.” Maren laughed again, this time softer, a little relieved, and explained that her tics were almost always related to plants or bugs, a quirk her neurologist said came from spending 90% of her waking hours thinking about pollinators. She had motor tics too, she said: shoulder jerks, three quick finger snaps, a sharp nod of the head, but the vocal tics were the ones that made people stare the most. She stayed for two hours that day, flipping through the field manual and taking notes in a beat-up leather notebook covered in bee stickers, and when she left, she pressed a monarch butterfly sticker into the palm of his hand as a thank you. Elias stuck that sticker on the corner of his name tag the second she was gone, and it stayed there, faded and peeling at the edges, for the next two years. Maren came back every Tuesday after that, always at 10 a.m., always wearing overalls, always bringing him a small gift: a jar of wild blackberry jam she’d made, a pressed milkweed bloom, a sticker of a bumblebee holding a tiny book. Elias started saving her rare botanical books as soon as they came in, tucking them behind the desk so no one else could check them out, and he started looking forward to Tuesdays more than any other day of the week, more than his monthly bookbinding workshop, more than the weekend video game marathons with Leo, more than the chamomile tea he brewed every morning. He’d never admit it to his sister, but his carefully curated routine had started to revolve around Maren, and he didn’t mind one bit.
